div.p: Naso, by now no stranger as a dweller in the Tomitan land, sends you this work from the Getic shore. If you have leisure, Brutus, take in these foreign little books as guests, and hide them away in any place at all. They dare not come within the public monuments, lest their own author should have barred that road to them. Ah, how often I have said: 'You teach nothing shameful, surely: go, that place lies open to chaste verses!' Yet they do not approach, but, as you see yourself, they think it safer to lie hidden beneath a private household god, You ask where you can set these down without offending anyone? Where the Art of Love once stood, that space lies vacant for you. You may ask, perhaps, under the very newness of the thing, why they come. Take it, whatever it is, so long as it is not love. You will find, although the title is not a piteous one, this no less sorrowful than that which I gave before. The matter is the same, the title differs; and the letter shows to whom it is sent, the name not being concealed. You do not wish this, but neither can you forbid it, and the dutiful Muse comes to those who do not want her. Whatever it is, add it to my works. Nothing prevents those born in exile, with the laws kept, from enjoying the city. There is nothing for you to fear. Antony's writings are read, and learned Brutus keeps his book-cases ready to hand. Nor in my madness do I match myself with names so great: I did not bear cruel arms against the gods. In short, Caesar's name, though he himself does not demand it, is missing from no book of mine without its honour. If you doubt me, admit the praises of the gods, and take my poem with the name removed. The branch of peace-bringing olive helps in war: will it profit nothing to have the author of peace at hand? When Aeneas's neck was bent beneath his father, the very flame is said to have given the man a way through: the book carries the son of Aeneas, and shall not every road lie open? But this man is the father of his country; that other was his own father's. Is anyone so bold that he would force from his threshold one who shakes the jingling rattles with a Pharian hand? When the piper before the Mother of the gods plays on his curved horn, who refuses the coin of a small alms? We know that nothing of the sort is done by command of Diana: yet the prophet has the means by which to live. The very deities of the gods above move our hearts, and it is no shame to be taken by such trust. Behold, in place of the rattle and the bored Phrygian boxwood I bear the holy names of the Julian race. I prophesy and admonish: make room for one who brings the sacred things! This honour is sought not for me, but for the great god. And although I deserved and felt the prince's anger, do not think that he himself wishes not to be worshipped by me. I have seen one confess he had profaned the deity of linen-clad Isis, and sit before Isiac altars, another, deprived of sight for a fault like his, cried out in the midst of the road that he had earned it. The powers of heaven rejoice that such proclamations are made, to prove by a witness how much their deities avail. Often they lighten punishments and restore stolen eyes, when they see that one has truly repented of his sin. I repent, oh! if anything of the wretched is believed by anyone, I repent, and am tortured myself by my own deed. And though it is exile, my fault is more grievous to me; and to suffer the penalty is less than to have earned it. Though the gods favour me, to whom he himself is more manifest, the penalty can be taken away, the fault will be everlasting. Death will surely bring it about that, when it comes, I be no exile: that I never sinned, death too will not bring about. It is no wonder, then, if my mind, made wasted, melts away like water flowing from the snow, as a ship is eaten when spoiled by the hidden ship-worm, as the wave hollows the rocks with the salt of the sea, as iron, laid by, is gnawed by rough rust, as a book stored away is consumed by the mouth of the moth, so my breast has the perpetual bites of cares, by which, with no end, it is worn away. Nor will these goads leave my mind sooner than life, and the one who grieves will fall sooner than the grief itself. If the gods above, to whom all that we are belongs, believe this of me, perhaps I shall be held worthy of some small aid, and I shall be moved into a place free from the Scythian bow. If I should pray for more than this, hard men, I shall be too bold of speech.

Hither too has come the fame of Caesar's triumph, where the languid breeze of the weary South wind scarcely comes. I thought nothing would be sweet to me in the Scythian region: now this place is less hateful than it was before. At last, the cloud of cares driven off, I saw some clear sky, and gave the lie to my own fortune. Though Caesar should be unwilling that any joys fall to me, yet he can wish this one thing to be granted to anyone. The gods too, that they may be worshipped by all with cheerful piety, bid sadness be laid aside through their festivals. In short—and it is sheer madness to dare to confess it— I shall enjoy this gladness, though he himself forbid it. As often as Jupiter aids the fields with useful showers, the clinging burr is wont to grow mingled with the crop. We too, a useless weed, feel the fruit-bearing deity, and are often helped by aid we did not seek. The joys of Caesar's mind are mine in my manly portion: that house has nothing private about it. Thanks to you, Rumour, through whom the pageant of the triumph, beheld, was mine, shut in among the Getae. With you as informer I learned that lately the countless nations had come together to be seen at the face of their leader! And that Rome, which holds the boundless world within her vast walls, scarcely had room for her guests. You told me that, when for many days before the cloudy South wind had poured down constant rains, by heaven's deity the sun shone clear, the day matching the people's countenance, and that thus the victor, with the honour of a great voice, gave the gifts of war to the praised men, and, about to take up the embroidered robes, bright insignia, first laid incense upon the holy hearths, and chastely appeased the justice of his own father, who has always a temple in that breast, and that, wherever the fortunate one went, the omen was joined to applause, and the stones blushed with sprinkled roses; straightway there were images in silver imitating overthrown walls, barbarian towns carried along with painted men, and rivers and mountains and battles in deep woods, and arms mingled with their own weapons in a heap, and from the gold of trophies, which the sun set ablaze, the roofs of the Roman Forum were golden, and that so many leaders bore chains added to their captive necks, almost as many as had been enough to be enemies. The greatest part of these gained life and pardon, among them too Bato, the sum and head of the war. Why should I deny that the deity's anger toward me can be lessened, when I see that the gods are mild to enemies? This same report has brought to us, Germanicus, that towns went under the title of your name. And that against you neither by mass of wall nor by arms nor enough by the cunning of the place were they safe. May the gods grant you years, for you will get the rest from yourself, let there be only long time for your valour. What I pray will come to pass: the oracles of bards are something: for the god has given favourable signs to one who prays, You too as victor Rome shall joyfully behold mounting the Tarpeian heights with garlanded horses; and a father shall watch the ripe honours of his son, receiving the joys which he himself gave to his own. Even now mark these words spoken to you by me, prophesying, greatest of young men in war and in the toga. This triumph too perhaps I shall record in poems, if only life suffice for my ills, if I do not myself first steep the Scythian arrows, and the fierce Getan carry off this head with his sword. And if your laurel be given to the temples while I am safe, you will say that twice my omens have been true.

Sea first beaten by the oars of Jason, and you, land, that lack neither fierce foe nor snow, will there be a time when I, Naso, shall leave you, bidden to be far off in a less hostile place? Or must I live forever in that barbarism, and be buried in the Tomitan soil? By your leave, if any leave is yours, Pontic land, which the neighbouring foe wears down on his swift horse, by your leave I would say it: you are the worst part of my hard exile, you weigh down my ills. You feel no spring girt with a flowering garland, you see no naked bodies of harvesters, nor does autumn hold out to you the vine-clad grapes: but an immoderate cold holds all the seasons, you keep the straits bound with ice, and in the sea the fish, shut in, has often swum beneath a roof of water. Nor have you springs, save almost of brackish water, which when drunk leaves it doubtful whether it stays or feeds the thirst, rare, and not fruitful, in the open fields stands out a tree, and on the land there is another form of the sea. No bird sings, unless one, far off in the woods, drinks the sea waters with hoarse throat, gloomy wormwood bristles over the empty plains, a bitter harvest suited to its own place. Add fears, and that the wall is battered by the foe, and the arrow drips, dipped in deadly poison, that this region is far off and out of the way of every road, and no one goes safe by foot or by ship. It is no wonder, then, if I seek an end of these things, and another soil is ever begged for me. It is more a wonder that you do not overcome this, my wife, and can hold back tears amid my ills. You ask what you should do? You should ask this very thing, of course, you will find it, if you truly wish to find out. To wish is too little: you must desire, that you may gain the end, and let this care make your sleeps short, I think many wish it: for who is so unjust to me as to wish my exile to lack peace? It befits you to lean with your whole breast and all your sinews and to strive for me by night and by day. And though others help, you ought to surpass my friends, wife, and come first to your own part. A great character has been laid on you by my little books: you are said to be the example of a good wife. Take care you do not fall away from it, that my heralding may be true; see that you guard the work of your fame. Though I myself complain of nothing, fame, silent, will complain of me, unless the care of me, which it owes, has been yours. Fortune has exposed me to be seen by the people, and has given more notice of me than there was before. Capaneus has been made better known by the lightning's stroke, Amphiaraus is known by his horses sunk in the earth, had he wandered less, Ulysses would be less known: great is the fame of Philoctetes by his own wound. If there is any place for the small among names so great, my ruin too makes me conspicuous, nor does my page suffer you to be unknown, by which you have a name no lower than Coan Bittis, whatever you do, then, you will be watched on a great stage, and you will be a dutiful wife before not a few witnesses. Believe me, as often as you are praised in my song, he who reads these praises asks whether you deserve them, and as I think more men favour those virtues, so not a few women will wish to carp at your deeds. See that you give them no chance that envy can say 'she is slow in seeking the safety of her wretched husband.' And since I fail, and cannot draw the chariot, make that you alone sustain the feeble yoke. Sick, I look to the physician with failing veins: while the last part of my soul remains to me, be present; and what I would render, if I myself were the stronger, that render to me, since you yourself are the more vigorous. Wedded love and the marriage compact demand this: by your own character, wife, you yourself demand it. This you owe to the house by which you are reckoned, that you may honour it no more by services than by probity, though you do all things, unless you are a praiseworthy wife, Marcia cannot be believed to be honoured by you. Nor am I unworthy: nor, if you wish to confess the truth, is no gratitude owed to my deserts. That is repaid me indeed with great interest, nor has rumour, even if it wished, the power to harm you, but yet add this one thing to your former deeds, that you be eager on behalf of my ills. Labour that I may lie in a less hostile region, and let no part of your duty be lame. I ask great things, but not such as bring envy on the asker: and though you do not gain them, your repulse is safe. Nor be angry with me if so often, in my song, I beg you to do what you do, and to imitate yourself. The trumpeter is wont to spur on the brave, and the leader with his own voice urges on men who fight well. Your probity is known and witnessed for all time; let your valour too be not less than your probity. You need not take up the Amazon's axe for me, nor bear the cut-out shield in a light hand. A deity must be worshipped, not that he be made friendly to me, but that he be less angry than he was before. If there is no favour, your tears will become your favour. By this part you can move the gods, or by none. That these may not fail you is well provided for by my ills: my husband's lot gives you a rich abundance of weeping; and as my affairs are, you will weep, I think, at every time. This wealth my fortune ministers to you. If my death had to be redeemed by yours, which I abhor, the wife of Admetus, whom you would follow, was there. You would become a rival of Penelope, if, chaste by craft, as a bride you wished to deceive the pressing suitors. If as companion you would follow the shade of your dead husband, Laodamia would be the leader of your deed. The daughter of Iphis would have to be set before your eyes, if you wished by chance to cast your body upon the kindled pyres. There is no need of death, none of the daughter of Icarius's web. Caesar's wife must be entreated by your mouth, who excels by her virtue, lest ancient antiquity press our age with the praise of chastity: who, having the beauty of Venus, the character of Juno, alone has been found worthy of a heavenly bed. Why do you tremble and fear to approach? Not impious Procne nor the daughter of Aeëtes is to be moved by your voice, nor the daughter-in-law of Egypt, nor Agamemnon's savage wife, nor Scylla, who terrifies the Sicilian waters with her loins, nor the parent of Telegonus, born to change shapes, nor Medusa, her knotted locks entwined with snakes, but the first of women, in whom Fortune proves that she can see, and has borne the false charges of being blind: than whom the world has nothing brighter on earth, from the sun's rising to its setting, Caesar excepted, choose a time often watched for, of asking, that your ship may not go out on an adverse tide. Not always do the oracles render the sacred lots, and the shrines themselves do not lie open at every time, when the state of the city is such as I now augur it to be, and no grief of the people contracts faces, when the house of Augustus, to be honoured as the Capitol, is glad, as it is and may it be, and full of peace, then may the gods grant you a chance of approaching, then think your words will accomplish something. If she is doing anything greater, defer your beginnings and beware of dashing my hope by haste. Nor again do I bid you wait until she is most at leisure: she scarcely has leisure for the care of her own body. . . . through the throng of affairs you too must go. When it has fallen to you to approach the face of Juno, see that you are mindful of the character you maintain. And do not defend my deed; a bad cause must be kept silent. Let your words be nothing but anxious prayers, then there must be no delay in tears, and, prostrate on the ground, stretch your arms toward those not mortal feet. Then seek nothing else but that I withdraw from the savage foe; let it be enough that Fortune is my foe. Many things indeed come to mind, but, confused by fear, even these you will scarcely be able to speak with trembling voice. I suspect this will be no loss to you. She will perceive that you greatly dreaded her majesty. Nor, if your words are broken by weeping, will it harm: sometimes tears have the weight of a voice, see too that a good day attend such beginnings and a fitting hour and a favouring omen. But first, fire laid on the holy altars, bring incense and pure wine to the great gods. Of these, before all, worship the Augustan deity and the dutiful offspring and the partner of his bed. Would that they may be mild to you in their accustomed way, and look upon your tears with no harsh faces.

Receive, Pompeius, a song drawn out from him who is debtor, Sextus, to you for his life. Who, whether you do not forbid your name to be set down by me, this sum too will be added to your deserts: or whether you frown, I shall confess indeed that I have sinned, yet the cause of my offence must be approved. My mind could not be held back from being grateful. May your anger, I pray, not be heavy upon a dutiful service. Oh, how often I have seemed to myself, in those books, impious, that you were read in no place! Oh, how often, when I wished to write another name, my hand, unknowing, brought yours to the wax! The very error in such mistakes pleased me, and the erasure was scarcely made by an unwilling hand, 'Let him see to it! In sum,' I said, 'let him complain himself! I am ashamed not to have earned this offence before.' Give me, if there is any, the Lethe that dulls the breast. Yet I shall not be able to be forgetful of you. And this I beg you to allow, and do not repel my words, disdained, nor think a crime is in my service, and let this slight gratitude be returned for deserts so great: if less, even against your will I shall be grateful. Never was your favour slow to my affairs, nor did your coffer deny me its bountiful wealth. Now too, in no way terrified by my sudden fate, your clemency brings and will bring aid to my life. You ask perhaps whence so great a confidence in the future is mine? Each man guards the work that he has made. As Venus is the labour and glory of the Coan artist, who presses her hair, wet with the sea's spray: as the warlike goddess, guardian of the Actaean citadel, whether of ivory or of bronze, stands, made by Phidias's hand: as Calamis claims the praise of the horses which he made: as the heifer, like the true one, is the work of Myron: so I, not the least part of your affairs, Sextus, am called the gift and work of your guardianship.

Maximus, you who fill the full measure of so great a name, and ennoble your line by your soul's nobility, you through whom it was possible to be born, although three hundred fell, since one day did not carry off all the Fabii, perhaps you ask by whom this letter is sent, and would wish to be more certain who it is that speaks with you, Ah me, what shall I do? I fear that, the name once read, you may read the rest harshly and with averted mind. See: I will dare to confess that I have written to you . . . I, who, though I confess I was worthy of a heavier penalty, can scarcely suffer heavier things. I am set in the midst of enemies and amid dangers, as if peace, along with my country, had been taken from me: men who, that they may double the causes of death by a savage wound, smear all their darts with viper's gall. Equipped with these, the horseman surveys the terrified walls like a wolf circling the penned-in sheep: and once the light bow is strung tight on the horse-hair cord, it stays always with its string unloosed. The roofs bristle, veiled as it were with fixed arrows, and the gate scarcely keeps off weapons with its firm bar. Add the look of the place, sheltered by neither leaf nor tree, and that idle winter is joined to winter. Here, fighting against the cold and against the arrows, and the fourth winter wearies me with my fate, my tears have no end, except when stupor blocks them: and a numbness like death holds my breast. Happy Niobe, although she saw so many deaths, who, turned to stone by her sufferings, laid aside all feeling! You too are happy, whose mouths, crying out for your brother, the poplar veiled in new bark! I am the man who cannot be admitted into any wood: I am the man who would wish, in vain, to be a stone. Though Medusa herself should come before my eyes, Medusa herself would lose her powers. We live so that we may never be without the bitter feeling, and my punishment grows heavier through the long delay. So the liver of Tityos, unconsumed and ever reborn, does not perish, that it may often be able to perish. But, I suppose, when rest and the common medicine of care, sleep, is near, night comes empty of its usual ills, Dreams terrify me, imitating real misfortunes, and my senses keep watch to my own harm. Either I seem to be dodging Sarmatian arrows, or to be giving my captive hands to harsh chains, or, when I am deceived by the image of a better sleep, I look upon the abandoned roofs of my own country. And now I talk much with you, friends whom I revered, and now with my dear wife. Thus when a brief and untrue pleasure has been grasped, that state of mine is made worse by the reminder of the good. Whether, then, the day looks upon this wretched head, or the frosty horses of Night are driven on, so my breast melts away with perpetual cares, as new wax does when fire is brought near it, Often I pray for death, and again I pray death away, that the Sarmatian soil may not cover my bones, when it comes to mind how great is Augustus's clemency, I believe that gentle shores can be granted after shipwreck. When I see how tenacious my fate is, I am broken, and slight hope, conquered by great fear, falls, yet I neither hope nor pray for anything further than to be able to escape this ill-changed place. This, or nothing, your favour might modestly attempt for me, with your honour kept safe. Take up the case, Maximus, eloquence of the Roman tongue, enter upon the defence of a difficult cause. It is a bad one, I confess, but it will become good with you pleading it, only speak gentle words on behalf of my wretched flight. For Caesar does not know, though a god knows all things, under what conditions this farthest place lies, Great labours of affairs occupy that deity: this is a care too small for a heavenly breast. He has no leisure to ask in what region the Tomitans are placed, a land scarcely known to the neighbouring Getae, or what the Sarmatae do, what the fierce Iazyges, and the Tauric land of Orestes's goddess, and what other nations, when the Hister has stiffened with cold, cross its hard back on a swift horse. The greatest part of these men care nothing for you, fairest Rome, nor fear the arms of the Ausonian soldier, their bows and full quivers give them courage, and the horse, fit for long courses, as each may please, and that they have learned long to endure thirst and hunger, and that the pursuing enemy will have no waters. The man's anger would not have sent me into that land, if this soil had been well enough known to him. He rejoices that neither I nor any Roman is taken by the enemy, and I least of all, to whom he himself was granting life. He was unwilling, as he could have been, to destroy me with the slightest nod. There is no need of any Getae against my fate, but neither did he find anything done by me deserving death, and he can be less hostile than he was. Even then he did nothing except what I myself forced him to do: his anger is almost more sparing even than my desert. May the gods therefore grant, of whom he himself is most just, that the kindly earth bring forth nothing greater than Caesar, and as the earth was under him, so may it be under Caesar, and pass on, handed down through the hands of his line. But do you, before so calm a judge, such as I too have felt him to be, open your lips for my tears. Do not ask that it go well with me, but that ill go more safely, and that my exile be far from the savage enemy, and that the life which the present deities have granted me the squalid Getan may not take away with drawn sword: in short, that if I die, I may enter a more peaceful field, and that my bones be not pressed by the Scythian soil, nor that—as is fitting, no doubt, for an exile—my ill-laid ashes be struck by the hoof of a Bistonian horse, and that, if any feeling survives after death, no Sarmatian shade may even terrify my Manes. These things, heard, could have moved Caesar's mind, Maximus, if they had moved yours first. Let your voice, I pray, soften Augustus's ears for me, that voice which is wont to aid trembling defendants, and with the accustomed sweetness of your learned tongue bend the heart of the man who equals the gods above. Theromedon will not be entreated for you, nor cruel Atreus, nor he who made his men fodder for his horses, but a prince slow to punish, swift to reward, who grieves whenever he is forced to be fierce, who has always conquered that he might spare the conquered, and who shut civil wars with an everlasting bar, who restrains many by fear of punishment, few by punishment, and rarely casts his thunderbolts, with reluctant hand. Therefore, as an orator sent to ears so calm, ask that our exile be nearer the homeland. I am the man who honoured you, whom the festive table was wont to see among your guests: I am he who led the wedding-song to your marriage fires, and sang verses worthy of a fortunate wedding, whose little books you were wont, I remember, to praise, except those which harmed their own master, to whom you sometimes read your writings as I marvelled: I am he to whom a bride was given from your house. Marcia approves her and, beloved always from her earliest years, has counted her among her own companions, and before her the maternal aunt of Caesar held her so: those of whose judgment any woman is approved, is virtuous. Even Claudia, better than her own reputation, with these for her praisers, would have had no need of divine aid. We too have passed the years gone by without a stain: the latter part of my life must be passed over in silence. But to say nothing of myself, my wife is your burden: you cannot, with faith kept whole, disown her, she flees to you, she embraces your altars —each rightly comes to the gods who are honoured by him— and weeping she begs that, Caesar softened by your prayers, her husband's grave be made nearer.

He who from his first years has been a worshipper of your house, Naso, driven to the left shore of the Euxine sea, sends from the untamed Getae this greeting, Messalinus, which, present, he was wont to bring you. Ah me, if your face, on reading the name, is not what it was, and you hesitate to read the rest through! Read it through, and do not banish my words along with me: my verses may be in your city, though I may not. I did not, had Ossa borne Pelion, conceive that the bright stars could be touched by my hand, nor did we, following the mad camp of Enceladus, move arms against the gods, the lords of all things, nor, as the rash hand of the son of Tydeus did, were any deities assailed by my weapons. My fault is grievous, but one which dared to ruin me alone, and undertook no greater impiety. I can be called nothing but unwise and timid: these two are the true names of my mind. That I have deserved, after Caesar's anger, to find you too, by right, hard to my prayers, I confess; and such is your piety toward the whole name of Iulus, that you think yourself wounded when anyone is wounded thereby, But though you bear arms and threaten savage wounds, yet you will not make me fear you. The Trojan ship took in the Greek Achaemenides, and the Pelian spear helped the Mysian leader. Sometimes the violator of a temple flees to its altar, and does not shudder to seek the help of the offended deity. Someone may say that this is not safe. I admit it. But my ship does not go through calm waters, let others seek safe things: most wretched fortune is safe, for the fear of a worse outcome is absent, he who is swept away by the foaming brine, stretching out his arms, holds out his hands toward thorns and hard rocks, and the bird, fearing the hawk, with trembling wings dares, wearied, to come to human bosoms, nor does the hind, fleeing in terror from the hostile hounds, hesitate to trust herself to a neighbouring roof, Grant access, I pray, most gentle one, to my tears, and do not bar the rigid door against my timid words, and carry my words, favouring, to the Roman deities, worshipped by you no less than the Thunderer of the Tarpeian rock, and, as envoy of my charge, take up the cause: though no cause is good that goes by my name. Already near laid out, surely now cold and sick, I shall, saved through you—if only I am saved—be safe. Now let your favour, which the eternal prince's love grants you, strive on behalf of my weary affairs. Now let that home-bred brightness of your eloquence be with you, by which you could be of use to trembling defendants. For your eloquent father's tongue lives on in you, and that gift has found its heir. This I implore, not that it try to defend me; the cause of a confessed defendant must not be guarded. But whether you should excuse my deed by the origin of error, or whether it profit nothing to stir such a thing, see. It is the kind of wound which, since it is not curable, I think it is safer not to handle. Tongue, be silent! There is nothing further to be told. I would wish I could bury my own ashes myself. So, then, as if no error had deceived me, speak your words, that I may enjoy the life he himself gave; and when he is serene and has relaxed those features which move the lands and the empire along with themselves, beg that he not let me be a small prey to the Getae, and that he grant a gentle soil to my wretched flight. The time suits prayers: he is strong, and sees what strength, Rome, he has made yours. His consort, safe, keeps her marriage couch; his son advances the Ausonian empire; Germanicus himself surpasses his years in spirit, nor is the vigour of Drusus less than his nobility, add that the dutiful daughters and granddaughters and the sons of grandsons and the other members of the Augustan house are well; add the Paeonians lately triumphed over, add to quiet the arms of mountainous Dalmatia subdued. Nor did Illyria, her arms cast away, disdain to bear Caesar's foot on her servile head, he himself, conspicuous above the chariot with calm face, bore his temples bound with the Phoebean maiden. Him, as he went, your dutiful offspring accompanied, worthy of their parent and of the names bestowed, like the brothers whom, holding the neighbouring temple, the deified Julius sees from his lofty shrine. To these Messalinus does not deny the first place of his gladness, to whom all things must yield, whatever is left over from these comes into the contest of love: in this part he will be second to no man. He will honour this day before that on which, as decreed to the deserving, the laurel comes worthy of honoured locks. Happy those who, oh, were allowed to behold the triumphs and to enjoy the gods in the face of a leader who equals them! But for me, instead of Caesar's face, there are Sarmatians to see and a land destitute of peace and water bound with ice. If, however, you hear these things and my voice reaches there, let your favour be coaxing toward changing my place. This that father of yours, cultivated by me from earliest youth, asks, if an eloquent shade has any feeling. This your brother asks too, though perhaps he fears lest the care of saving me harm you. The whole house asks this, nor can you yourself deny that I too was a part of your throng. At least of my talent, which I felt I used ill, the Art of Love excepted, you were often an approver. Nor can my life, if you take away only the latest sins, be shameful to your house. So, then, may the inner shrines of your race flourish, and may you be a care to the gods above and to the Caesars. Worship that deity, mild, but justly angry with me, that he may take me from the savagery of the Scythian place. It is hard, I confess, but valour strives toward steep things, and the gratitude for such a service will be greater. Yet it is not the Aetnaean Polyphemus in his vast cave, nor Antiphates, who will receive your words, but a calm and easy father, ready to pardon, and one who often thunders without the lightning's fire, who, when he has decreed something sad, becomes sad himself, and for whom to inflict punishment is almost his own punishment. Yet his clemency was conquered by my fault, and his anger, forced to it, came to its full strength. And since I am removed from my country by the whole world's width, and may not fall prostrate before the very gods, carry these charges, as priest, to the powers above whom you worship, but add your own prayers too to my words. Yet make this attempt only if you think it will not harm. You will be pardoned. Shipwrecked, I fear every sea.

The greeting which you read sent to you from me, Cotta, I pray it may be sent as truly as it has arrived. For, safe, you take much from my torments, and you make a good part to be safe in me. And while some falter and leave the tossed sails, you alone remain the anchor of my shattered craft. Welcome, then, is your piety; I forgive those who, when Fortune did, turned their backs in flight, when the thunderbolts strike one, they terrify not one, and the throng beside the smitten man is wont to be afraid: and when a wall has given signs of coming ruin, that place is left empty by anxious fear. Who, of the timid, does not shun the sick man's contagion, fearing lest the neighbouring ill draw harm from there? Me too some of my friends abandoned out of excessive terror and fear, not out of hatred. They lacked not piety, not the will to do their duty: they dreaded the gods who were against me. And as they can seem more cautious and timid, so they did not deserve to be called bad. Or my candour so excuses my dear friends, that, that they may have no charges against me, it favours them: let these be content with pardon, and let them boast that their deed is cleared, with even me as witness. You are the better, the few, who in hard straits thought it shameful to bring me no help. Then, therefore, the gratitude for your service will die, when I have become ash, my body consumed. I am wrong, and it will outlast the times of my life, if only I am read by a mindful posterity. Bloodless bodies are owed to mournful tombs: name and honour escape the built-up pyres. Both Theseus died and he who accompanied Orestes: but yet each lives on in his own praises. You too late grandsons will often praise, and your glory will be bright in my writings. Here too the Sarmatians and the Getae now know you, and the barbarian throng approves such hearts, and when I lately told of your probity (for I have learned to speak Getic and Sarmatian), by chance a certain old man, as he stood in that gathering, gave such words in answer to my sounds: 'We too, good guest, know the name of friendship, we whom the Pontus and the Hister hold far from you. There is a place in Scythia, the men of old called it Tauris, which is not so very far from the Getic soil. In this land (and I am not ashamed of my country) I was born: that nation worships the goddess who shares with Phoebus. The temples remain today, leaning on vast columns, and one goes up to them by forty steps, fame reports that there was a heavenly image there; and, that you may doubt it less, the base stands bereft of its goddess; and the altar, which had been by nature white of stone, discoloured, is red, stained with poured blood. A woman performs the rites, not known to the wedding torch, who surpasses the Scythian women in nobility, the kind of sacrifice is this, so the fathers ordained, that a stranger fall slain by a virgin's sword. Thoas held the realm, famous on the Maeotic shore, nor was any other better known on the Euxine waters. With him holding the sceptre, they say that one Iphigenia made a journey through the clear air. Whom, borne by light winds beneath a cloud through the sky, Phoebe is believed to have set down in these places. She had ruled over the temple duly for many years, performing the grim rites with unwilling hand: when two young men came on a sail-bearing ship and pressed our shores with their feet. Equal was their age and their love, of whom one was Orestes, the other was Pylades: fame holds the names. At once they are led to the cruel altar of Trivia, their two hands bound behind their backs, the Greek priestess sprinkles the captives with lustral water, that the long fillet may wreathe their tawny locks. And while she prepares the rite, while she veils her temples with bands, while she herself invents reasons for the slow delay, "I am not cruel, young men (forgive me)," she said, "I perform rites more barbarous than my own land. This is the custom of the nation. Yet from what city do you come? Or on what journey have you sought, with an ill-omened ship?" She spoke, and the dutiful maiden, hearing the name of her homeland, learned that they were sharers of her own city. "Let one of you," she said, "fall as victim to the rites, let the other go as messenger to his father's seat." Pylades, ready to perish, bids dear Orestes go; he refuses, and each in turn contends to die. This one thing arose, in which they did not agree: in all else they were a harmonious pair, and without strife. While the fair young men carry on the contest of love, she scratches written marks to her brother. She gave charges to her brother, and he to whom they were given (behold the chances of men!) was her brother. Without delay, they snatch the images of Diana from the temple, and secretly are borne by ship over the vast waters. Wondrous the love of the young men. Though so many years have passed, in Scythia even now they have a great name.' After this common tale was told by him, all praised the deeds and the dutiful faith, no doubt on this shore too, than which none is fiercer, the name of friendship moves barbarian hearts, what ought you, born in the Ausonian city, to do, when such deeds touch the harsh Getae? Add that your mind is always mild, and your character holds the token of high nobility, which Volesus, founder of your father's name, would acknowledge, which Numa on your mother's side would not deny to be his own. And the added Cottae prove it for your inherited names, a house that would perish if you were not. Worthy man of this lineage, think that to succour a fallen friend befits that character of yours.

What you read, O greatest bard of great kings, comes from the unshorn Getae, Severus: whose name that my little books have so far kept silent, if only you allow me to speak the truth, I am ashamed. Yet a letter, bereft of verse, never ceased to go, dutiful, by alternate turns, only songs attesting my mindful care for you have not been given. For what should I give that you yourself make? Who would give honey to Aristaeus, who Falernian wine to Bacchus, corn to Triptolemus, fruit to Alcinous? You have a fertile breast, and among those who dwell on Helicon to no one does that crop come forth more richly. To send a song to this man was to add leaves to the woods, this was the cause, Severus, of my delaying. Nor yet does my talent answer me as before, but I plough a dry shore strewn with the ploughshare. No doubt, as mud blinds the channels in the waters, and the harmed water stops, its spring suppressed, so my breast is spoiled by the mud of ills, and my song flows from a poorer vein. If anyone had set Homer himself in this land, he too, believe me, would have become a Getan. Grant pardon to the confession, I have loosed the reins of my studies too, and a letter is rarely drawn by my fingers. That sacred impulse which nourishes the breasts of bards, which used to be in me before, is absent, the Muse scarcely comes to her parts, scarcely, the tablets taken up, does she lay her sluggish hands on them, almost forced, and small, not to say no, pleasure in writing is mine, nor does it delight me to bind words in numbers, whether because I have gained no fruits from this at all, so that that thing should be the beginning of my ill: or because to make rhythmic gestures in the dark, and to write a song you might read to no one, is the same. A hearer rouses zeal, and praised valour grows, and glory has an immense spur. Here to whom should I recite my writings, but the yellow-haired Coralli, and what other nations the barbarous Hister holds? But what should I do alone, and with what material should I waste my unhappy leisure, and steal away the day? For since neither wine nor the deceiving dice holds me, through which the silent time is wont to slip away unseen, nor does the land, renewed by its tillage—which I should desire, if it were allowed amid the fierce wars—delight me, what, except the Muses, cold comforts, remains, goddesses who have not deserved well of me? But you, for whom the Aonian spring is more happily drunk, love the study which usefully yields to you, and worthily honour the sacred rites of the Muses, and that I may read it, send here some work of your recent care.

Your Naso sends you this greeting, Rufinus, a wretched man, if a wretched man can belong to anyone. The consolations lately given to my troubled mind brought aid and hope to my ills, and as the hero, son of Poeas, felt by the arts of Machaon the healing help when his wound was soothed, so I, lying low in mind and wounded by a bitter blow, began to be stronger at your reminder, and, already failing, so revived at your words as a vein is wont to return when wine is poured in. Yet your eloquence did not show such great powers that my breast should be made whole by your words. Though you draw much from the whirlpool of my care, no less than what is drained will be left over. In long time, perhaps, a scar will be drawn over: raw wounds shudder at hands brought near. It is not always in the physician's power for the sick man to be relieved: sometimes the malady is stronger than skilled art. You see how blood released from the soft lung leads by a certain path to the Stygian waters, though the man of Epidaurus himself bring sacred herbs, he will heal the wounds of the heart by no aid. Medicine knows not how to take away the knotty gout, nor does it help against the dreaded waters of dropsy. Care too is sometimes curable by no art— or, if it be so, it must be thinned out by long delay. When your precepts had well steadied my fallen spirit, and the armour of your breast had been taken up by me, again the love of country, stronger than all reason, undid the work which your writings had done. Whether you wish this to be called dutiful affection or womanish, I confess that in my wretchedness my heart is soft. The wisdom of the Ithacan is not doubtful, and yet he longs to be able to see the smoke from his fathers' hearths. By some sweetness or other one's native soil draws all men, and does not let them be forgetful of it. What is better than Rome? What worse than the Scythian cold? Yet hither the barbarian flees from that city, though the daughter of Pandion is well kept in her cage, she strives to return into her own woods. Bulls seek their accustomed glades, lions their accustomed lairs— nor does their wildness hinder them from seeking their dens. You, nevertheless, hope that the bites of exile can yield from my breast to your soothing remedies. Bring it about that you yourselves be not so dear to me, that it may be a lighter ill to have lost such friends, But, I suppose, though I lack the land in which I was born, it has at least fallen to me to be in a human place. I lie deserted on the sands of the world's edge, where the buried earth bears perpetual snows. No field here brings forth fruit, no sweet grapes, no willows are green on the bank, no oaks on the hill. Nor should you praise the sea more than the land: the waters always, empty of suns, swell with the rage of the winds. Wherever you look, the plains lie lacking a tiller, and vast fields, which no one claims, lie waste. The enemy is at hand, to be feared on the right and on the left, and with the dread of his nearness terrifies both flanks, one side is to feel Bistonian pikes, the other, darts hurled by a Sarmatian hand. Go now and recite to me the examples of men of old who bore their lot with a brave mind, and admire the grave strength of great-souled Rutilius, who did not use the offered terms of return. Smyrna held the man, not Pontus and a hostile land, Smyrna, scarcely less to be sought than any place. The Cynic of Sinope did not grieve to be far from his country, for he chose your seats, land of Attica. The son of Neocles, who crushed Persian arms with arms, felt his first exile in an Argive city, Aristides, driven from his country, fled to Lacedaemon, between which two it was doubtful which should rank first. Patroclus as a boy left Opus after a murder done, and came as a guest to the Thessalian soil of Achilles. The exile from Haemonia withdrew to the Pirenian wave, under whose guidance the sacred timbers ran on the Colchian water. Cadmus, son of Agenor, left the Sidonian walls, that he might set his walls in a better place. Tydeus, banished from Calydon, came to Adrastus, and the land dear to Venus received Teucer. Why should I tell of the ancients of the Roman race, among whom Tibur was the farthest land for exiles? Though I follow them all out, to no one in all the ages has so distant from his country or more dreadful a place been given. So much the more let your wisdom pardon me in my grief: it does, not so very much, what your words require. Yet I do not deny that, if my wounds could close, they could close by your precepts. But I fear that you labour to save me in vain, and that, hopeless and sick, I am not helped by the aid brought near. Nor do I say this because there is greater wisdom in me, but because I am better known to myself than to a physician. Yet, however that may be, your great kindness, your goodwill, reaches me, and is taken in good part.

Maximus, you who match your name by your bright virtues, and do not let your talent be crushed by your nobility, honoured by me—for how does this state differ from death, to the very last moment of my life— you do a thing, not turning away from a friend in rough garb, than which none is rarer in your age. It is shameful to say, but, if only we confess the truth, the common crowd approves friendships by their usefulness, the care of what is profitable comes before what is honourable, and faith stands and falls with fortune. Nor would you easily find, among many thousands, one who thinks virtue is its own reward. Right action's very beauty, if rewards are lacking, does not move them, and to be honest for nothing is regretted. Nothing is dear unless it profits: but take from the greedy mind the hope of fruit, and no one will be worth seeking. But now each man loves his own returns, and what may be useful to him he reckons up on anxious fingers. That once venerable deity of friendship is on sale, and sits for hire like a harlot, the more I marvel that you too are not drawn, as by rushing waters, into the corruption of the common vice, no one is loved unless his fortune is favourable: which, as soon as it thunders, puts all those nearest to flight. Behold me, once fenced about by not a few friends, while a favourable breeze blew on my sails, when the wild seas swelled with the cloudy wind, I am left in the midst of the waters with a shattered ship, and though others were unwilling even to seem to know me, scarcely two or three of you brought help to me, cast away. Of whom you are the chief, for you were worthy to be not a follower, but a leader, not to seek an example, but to give one. You, confessing that I had committed nothing exactly save error, your probity and sense of duty aid of their own accord. With you as judge, virtue lacks reward and is to be sought for itself, unaccompanied by external goods, you think it shameful to drive off a friend because he is to be pitied, and that, because he is unhappy, he should cease to be yours. It is gentler to put a finger beneath the weary man's chin than to plunge the swimmer's face into the flowing waters. See what the grandson of Aeacus rendered to his friend after death: and reckon that this life of mine is like death. Theseus accompanied Pirithous to the Stygian waves: how far is my death from the Stygian water? The young Phocean stood by the mad Orestes: and my fault has no small share of madness, You too admit the praises of great men, as you do, and bring what help you can to the fallen. If I know you well, if you are now too what you used to be before, and your spirits have not fallen, the more Fortune rages, the more you yourself resist, and, as is fitting, you take care that she not conquer you; and, that you may fight well, the enemy, by fighting well, makes you do so. So the same cause both profits and harms me. No doubt, dearest of young men, you count it unworthy to be made a companion of the goddess that stands upon the world. You are firm, and since they are not such as you would wish, you steer the sails, whatever they are, of a shattered craft, and the ruin, which was so shaken that it is thought now about to fall, still remains, propped up by your shoulders. Your anger indeed at first had been just, nor milder than his who was offended at me by right. And whatever grief had touched the heart of high Caesar, you swore at once that it was your own. Yet when the origin of my disaster was heard by you, you are said to have groaned at my errors. Then first your letter began to console me and to give hope that the wounded god could be bent. Then the constancy of our long friendship moved you, which had begun for me before your birth, and that you were made others' friend, but born mine, and that I gave you in your cradle the first kisses. And since your house has been honoured by me always from tender years, it forces me to be an old burden to you. That father of yours, the eloquence of the Latin tongue, which was not inferior to his nobility, first urged me to dare to entrust my poems to fame: he was the leader of my talent. Nor do I claim that your brother could recall from what time he was first honoured by me. Yet you above all I have so embraced, that you alone in whatever chance were our chief favour, Aethalian Ilva last saw you with me, and received the tears falling from my cheeks in sorrow: when, as you asked whether the report was true which the evil rumour of my fault had brought, between confessing doubtfully and doubtfully denying, I hung, giving frightened signs out of fear, and like the snow which the watery South wind melts, the rising drop went down my stunned cheeks. Recalling these things, then, and seeing that my offences can lie hidden by the pardon of a first error, you look back on an old friend in his weary affairs, and aid my wounds with your soothing remedies. For which, if a chance of wishing be granted me, I would pray a thousand blessings on one who has deserved so well. But if your prayers alone be granted me, I shall pray that, Caesar being safe, your mother be safe for you. These things, when you made the altars rich with incense, I remember you were wont to ask of the gods first.

If you have leisure to give a little time to a fugitive friend, O star of the Fabian race, Maximus, be present, while I tell you what I saw, whether it was the shade of a body or the likeness of the true thing or that sleep. It was night, and the moon was entering the double-leaved windows, shining as bright as it is wont about the month's middle. Sleep, the common rest of cares, held me, and my languid limbs were spread over the whole couch, when suddenly the air, stirred by wings, shuddered, and the window, moved, groaned with a small sound. Terrified, I raise my limbs onto my left elbow, and sleep, driven off, departs from my fearful breast. Love stood there, not with the face he used to have before, sad, holding the bedpost of maple with his left hand, having no collar on his neck, no clasp in his hair, nor his locks well-arranged, adorned as before, his soft hair hung over his rough face, and his wing seemed rough to my eyes, such as is wont to be on the back of the airy dove, which, handled, many hands have touched. As soon as I knew him, for no other is better known to me, my tongue, set free, addressed him in such sounds: 'O boy, cause of exile to your deceived master, whom it would have been more useful for me not to have taught, have you come here too, where there is peace at no time, and the barbarous Hister meets with bound waters? What was your reason for the road, unless to see my ills? Which, if you know it not, are hateful to you. You first dictated to me my youthful songs: under your guidance I added five feet to six, and you did not allow me to rise to Maeonian song nor to tell the deeds of great leaders, perhaps your bow and your fires have lessened the slight, yet some, powers of my talent. For while I sang your kingdom and your parent's, my mind had no leisure for any great work, nor had this been enough: I made, with foolish song too, that you could be no novice in my Arts. For which exile has been rendered me, wretched, as reward, and that too in the farthest, peaceless places. But Eumolpus, son of Chione, was not such toward Orpheus, nor was Olympus such toward the Phrygian Satyr, nor did Chiron take such rewards from Achilles, and they say Numa did no harm to Pythagoras. And not to recount names gathered through long ages, I alone have perished by my very pupil. While I gave you arms, while I taught you, wanton one, this is the gift the master has from his pupil, yet you know, and could swear to say it plainly, that I did not stir up unlawful beds. I wrote these things for those whom neither the fillet touches on their chaste hair nor the long robe upon their feet, tell me, I pray, did you ever learn to deceive wives, and to make the line uncertain by my commands? Or is every woman strictly kept off from these little books whom the law forbids to have stolen lovers? Yet what does this profit, if, forbidden by a severe law, I am believed to have composed the notes of adultery? But you, so may you have arrows that smite all things, so may your torches never lack their swift fire, so may Caesar rule the empire and restrain all lands, who is yours through your brother Aeneas, bring it about that the anger be not implacable toward me, and that he be willing to punish me in a more agreeable place. This I seemed to have said to the winged boy, these sounds he seemed to me to have given: 'By my weapons, my torches, and by my weapons, my arrows, by my mother and by Caesar's head I swear, that you have learned nothing unpermitted from me, your master, and that no crime is in your Arts. And would that I could defend the rest as I defend this! You know there is something else, greater, that has harmed you, whatever it is (for the grief itself need not be recounted, nor can you say it is far from your fault) though you shadow the crime under the image of error, the judge's anger was not heavier than your desert. Yet, that I might see and console you as you lay, my wing glided over the immense roads. These places I then first saw, when, at my mother's asking, the Phasian maiden was pierced by my weapons. Why I now revisit them again after long ages, you make me do, O soldier friendly to my camp. Lay aside your fears, then: Caesar's anger will grow mild, and a softer hour will come to your prayers. And do not fear delay, the time we seek is at hand, and the triumph holds all things full of gladness, while his house and his sons, while his mother Livia rejoices, while you rejoice, great father of your country and of its leader, while the people congratulate themselves, and through the whole city every altar is warm with fragrant fires, while the venerable temple offers easy access, it must be hoped that our prayers can avail,' he spoke, and either he melted into the thin air, or my senses began to wake. If I doubted that you favour these words, O Maximus, I should think the swans were of Memnon's colour, but neither is the milky fluid changed to black pitch, nor does what was white become turpentine-wood from ivory. A nature suited to mine is yours, for you have a noble heart and the simplicity of Hercules, envy, a sluggish vice, does not climb to lofty characters, but, lurking, creeps like a viper on the lowest ground. Your mind, sublime, towers even above your race itself, nor have you a name grander than your talent. Therefore let others harm the wretched and wish to be feared, and carry darts dipped in biting gall: but your house is accustomed to aiding suppliants, in whose number, I pray, you would wish me to be.'

Shall I complain, or be silent? Shall I set down the crime without a name, or should I wish that who you are be known to all? I shall not use a name, lest you be commended by my complaint, and fame be sought for you by my song. While my ship was founded on a sound keel, you who wished to run with me were the first. Now, because Fortune has knit her brow, you withdraw, since you know there is need of your help. You even dissemble, and do not wish to seem to know me, and ask who Naso is, when you hear the name, I am that man, though you do not wish to hear it, joined to you, almost a boy to a boy, by an old friendship: I am he who first used to know your serious affairs and first to be present at your pleasant jests: I am the messmate, the familiar of close intimacy, I am the one Muse in your judgments. I am he, of whom now whether I live, faithless one, you know not, for whom you had no care to ask. Whether I was never dear, you confess you feigned: or, if you were not pretending, you will be found fickle. Or come, name some anger which has changed you: for unless yours is just, my complaint is just. What crime now forbids you to be like the man you were before? Or do you call it a crime, that I have begun to be wretched? If you brought me no help in affairs and deeds, a sheet marked with three words would have come. I scarcely believe it indeed, but report says that you even insult me as I lie low, and do not spare your words. What are you doing, ah, madman? Why, if Fortune should withdraw, do you yourself snatch away the tears for your own shipwreck? This goddess confesses by her unsteady wheel how fickle she is, who always has her summit beneath a doubtful foot, she is more uncertain than any leaf, than any breeze: equal to her in fickleness, base one, is your own alone. All things of men hang on a slender thread, and what once was strong falls by a sudden chance, who has not heard of the wealth of rich Croesus? Yet, taken by the foe, he kept his life, he lately feared in the Syracusan city scarcely repelled hard hunger by a humble art, what had been greater than Magnus? Yet he begged, fleeing, with a client's submissive voice, for aid. And the man to whom the whole world of lands obeyed, . . . he, famous for the Jugurthine and the Cimbrian triumph, in which, with him as consul, victorious Rome was so often, Marius lay in the mud and marsh reed, and that so great a man endured many shameful things. Divine power plays in human affairs, and the present hour scarcely has sure faith. If anyone had said to me 'You will go to the Euxine shore, and will fear to be struck by a Getan's bow,' 'Go, drink,' I should have said, 'the juices that purge the breast, and whatever is born in all Anticyra.' Yet I have suffered these things: nor, though I could guard against mortal things, could I beware the weapons of the highest god. You too, see that you fear, and what seems glad to you while you speak, think that it can become sad.

Already a worse age is sprinkled on me with grey hairs, and already the wrinkle of the old man ploughs my face. Already vigour and strength languish in my shaken body, nor do the games that pleased the young man please me. Nor, if you saw me suddenly, could you recognize me, so great has been the ruin of my age. I confess the years do this, but there is another cause too, the anguish of mind and continuous toil. For if anyone should reckon out my ills through long years, believe me, I shall be older than Pylian Nestor. You see how, in the hard fields—and what is firmer than an ox?— toil breaks the strong bodies of bulls. The soil, which has never been used to rest in fallow ground, grows old, wearied by constant fruits. A horse will die, if anyone goes always to the contests of the Circus with unintermitted courses, firm though she be, a ship will be loosened on the sea, which is never dry, never without the flowing waters. Me too the immense series of ills weakens, and forces me to be old before my time, Leisure nourishes the body, the mind too is fed by it: immoderate toil, on the contrary, wears away both. See, because the son of Aeson came into these parts, what praise he wins from late posterity. Yet his toil was both lighter and less than mine, if only great names do not bear down the truth, He set out for the Pontus with Pelias sending him, who was scarcely to be feared beyond the bounds of Thessaly. Caesar's anger has harmed me, before whom from the sun's rising to the sun's setting either land trembles. Haemonia is nearer than Rome to the Left Pontus, and he completed a shorter journey than I. He had as companions the foremost men of the Achaean land: but all forsook my flight. We furrowed the vast sea in a fragile ship: the keel that bore the son of Aeson was thick. Nor had I Tiphys as steersman, nor the son of Agenor to teach me which ways to flee and which to follow. Royal Juno guarded him along with Pallas: no deities defended my head, the stealthy arts of Cupid aided him; arts which I would wish Love had not learned from me. He returned home: we shall die in these fields, if the heavy anger of the offended god persists. Harder, then, is my toil, most faithful wife, than that which the son of Aeson underwent. You too, whom I left a young woman when I departed the city, it is likely have grown old amid my ills, Oh, may the gods grant that I be able to see you so, and to give dear kisses to your changed hair, and to embrace with my arms your body, not plump, and to say 'care for me has made this slender too,' and to tell you, weeping myself, my labours to one weeping, and to enjoy the conversation never hoped for, and to bring incense to the Caesars, and to the wife worthy of a Caesar, to true gods, with a mindful hand! Would that the mother of Memnon, the prince softened, might as soon as possible summon that day forth with rosy face!

Receive a conversation from Naso by the icy Hister, Atticus, not to be doubted in my judgment. Do you still remain mindful of your unhappy friend, or does your care, grown languid, desert its part? The gods are not so harsh to me that I could believe, or think it right, that you no longer remember me. Your image is always set before my eyes, and I seem to see your face in my mind. I recall many serious things shared with you, and not a few hours given to pleasant jests, often the hours, swift in long talk, seemed long, often the day was shorter than my words. Often a poem, just made, came to your ears and a new Muse was submitted to your judgment. What you had praised, I thought had pleased the people. This was the sweet reward of my guiding care. And that my book might be polished smooth by a friend's file, more than once an erasure was made at your prompting. The forums saw us together, every portico, the street, the curved theatres with their joined seats, in short, our love, dearest one, was always as great as was between the son of Aeacus and the son of Nestor. I would not, even if you drank cups of careless Lethe, believe that these things could fall from your breast. The long day will sooner come at the winter star, and the night, slower in winter, will be at the solstice, neither will Babylon have cold, nor the Pontus heat, and the marigold will conquer the Paestan roses in scent, sooner than forgetfulness of my affairs come over you. The white part of my fate is not so wholly null. Yet, lest this confidence can be called false and my belief foolish, take care, and with constant faith protect an old comrade, as far as is allowed and as much as I shall not be burdensome.

These words, bearing no empty greeting to you, your Naso sends from the Tomitan city, and he bids you favour his Triumph, Rufinus, if, however, it has come into your hands. It is a slight work, unequal to your preparations: yet such as it is, I ask you to protect it. Strong things are sound of themselves, and seek no Machaon. The doubtful sick man flees to the physician's aid. Great poets have no need of a kindly reader: they hold him, however unwilling and hard. We, whose talent long toils have lessened, or perhaps there never was any before, weak in strength, are strong by your candour: which, if you take from me, I should think all things snatched away. And though all my works lean on your favourable goodwill, that book has a special claim to pardon. Other bards have written of the triumph they beheld; it is something to mark with mindful hand what was seen. We have written these things scarce caught from the common rumour by an eager ear, and report was my eyes. No doubt like feelings, or the same impulse, comes from things heard as from things beheld! Nor do I complain of the gleam of silver and gold which you saw, which I lacked, nor of that purple: but the places, the nations shaped in a thousand figures and the battles themselves would have nourished my song, and the faces of kings, the surest pledges of the mind, would perhaps have aided that work somewhat. From the very applause of the people and their glad favour any talent can have grown warm: and I should have taken vigour at such a shout, as the raw soldier does at the trumpet heard for arms. Though my breast be colder than the snows and ice and colder than this place which I endure, that face of the leader standing in the ivory chariot would shake off all cold from my senses. Lacking these things and using doubtful authorities, I come by right of your favour to your aid. Neither the names of the leaders nor the names of the places were known to me, my hands had no material. What small fraction of so great affairs was there which fame could report or anyone could write to me? The more, O reader, you ought to pardon, if anything has been erred there or passed over by me. Add that my lyre, constantly practised in its master's complaints, was scarce turned to a glad song. Scarcely, after so long, did good words come to me as I sought them, and to rejoice in anything seemed a strange thing to me. And as the eyes shrink from the unaccustomed sun, so my mind was sluggish toward gladness. The newness of all things, too, is most dear, and the favour for a service which delay slows down is absent. The rest, vying, written about the great triumph, I suspect were long ago read by the people's mouth. That the thirsty reader drank, my cups when he was full: that was drunk fresh, my water will be lukewarm. I did not delay, nor did sloth make me late! The farthest shore of the vast strait holds me. While rumour comes here and the hurried verses are made and, once made, go to you, a year can pass. And it makes no small difference whether you pluck untouched rose-beds first, or, late, those almost left behind by another's hand. What wonder, the garden drained of its plucked flowers, if a garland worthy of your leader has not been made? I deprecate this: let no one think a bard's words spoken against his own songs! My Muse has spoken for herself. I have sacred rites in common with you, poets, if the wretched may be in your choir, and a great part of my soul, you have lived with me, friends: in this part I honour you, absent, even now. Let my songs, then, be commended to your favour, on whose behalf I cannot myself speak, writings please mostly after death, because envy is wont to harm the living and carp at them with unjust tooth. If to live ill is a kind of death, the earth delays me, and only the tomb is lacking to my fate. In short, though my work of care be blamed on every side, there will be no one who reproves my devotion. Though strength be lacking, yet the will must be praised: with this I augur the gods are content. This makes the poor man too come welcome to the altars, and a lamb please no less than a slaughtered ox. The matter too was so great that to halt at its height would have been a great burden to the bard of the Aeneadae. Even the soft elegies could not bear so vast a weight of triumph on their unequal wheels, what foot I should now use is a doubtful question with me: for a second triumph over you, Rhine, is at hand, the forebodings of stirred bards are not in vain. A laurel must be given to Jove, while the former one is still green. Nor do you read my words, who am removed to the Hister, its rivers ill-drunk by the unpacified Getae: that is a god's voice, a god is in my breast, these things I foretell and prophesy with a god as guide. Why do you delay, Livia, to prepare the chariot and pageant for the triumphs? The wars now give you no delays. Treacherous Germany throws down her condemned spears. Now you will say my weighty word has its omen. Believe it, and in a short time proof will be at hand: your son will double the honour, and will go, as before, with yoked horses. Bring out the purple to cast on the victorious shoulders: the crown itself can know the accustomed head: but let shields and helmets shine with gems and gold, and let trophies, lopped, stand over the bound men: let ivory towns be girt with turreted walls, and the feigned thing be thought to be done in the true manner. Let squalid Rhine, his hair loosened beneath broken reeds, carry his waters stained with blood, already the captive kings demand their barbarian insignia and the woven robes richer than their fortune, and what besides the unconquered valour of your kin, often prepared for you, often to be prepared, performs, O gods, at whose prompting I have spoken what shall come to pass, approve, I pray, my words with swift fulfilment.

No day is so wet with southern rains that the rain pours with unbroken waters, nor is any place so barren that in it there is not a useful herb mixed, mostly, with hard brambles. Heavy fortune has made nothing so pitiable that joys do not lessen the ill in some part. Behold, lacking home and homeland and the sight of my own, shipwrecked, driven onto the waters of the Getic shore, yet I have found a cause whereby I can spread out my face, and not remember my fortune. For, as I walked alone on the tawny sand, a wing seemed to have given a sound behind my back. I look back, nor was there a body that I could perceive, yet these words were received by my ear: 'Behold, I come to you as messenger of glad things, Fame, glided through the immense ways of the air. With Pompeius consul, than whom no other is dearer to you, the next year will be bright and happy.' She spoke, and when she had filled the Pontus with glad rumour, the goddess turned her course from here to other nations. But for me, my cares dispersed amid the new joys, the unjust harshness of this place fell away. Therefore when, two-headed Janus, you have unlocked the long year, and December has been driven from the sacred month, the purple of the highest honour will clothe Pompeius, that he may owe nothing to his own titles. Already I seem to see the halls almost burst by the throng, and the people hurt by the failing room, and the temples of the Tarpeian seat first approached by you, and the gods made easy to your vows, the snow-white oxen offer their necks to the sure axe, which the Faliscan grass nourished in its fields: and though you would wish all the gods, then these more earnestly, to be favourable to you, Caesar will be there with Jove. The senate-house will receive you, and the fathers, called by custom, will turn their ears to your words. When your voice has gladdened these with eloquent mouth, and, as is wont, the day has brought prosperous words, and you have given due thanks to the gods above along with Caesar (who will give a reason why you do so often), then you will seek home again, with the whole senate attending, the house scarcely holding the people's homage. Wretched me, that I shall not be seen in that throng, nor will my eyes be able to enjoy those things! What is allowed, absent, with such mind as I can, I shall see you: that mind will behold the face of its own consul, may the gods grant that at some time our name come into your mind, and that you say, 'alas! what is that wretched man doing?' If anyone brings me these words of yours, I shall confess straightway that my exile is gentler.

He who once was not the least among your friends, asks you, Maximus, Naso asks, that you read his words, in which cease to look for my old talent, lest you seem unaware of my exile. You see how leisure corrupts an idle body, how the waters take a taint unless they are moved, and whatever skill I had in leading on a poem fails, and is made less by inactive sloth. These very things which you read, if you believe me at all, Maximus, I write with a reluctant and scarcely compelled hand. It does not please me to strain my mind to such tasks, nor does the summoned Muse come to the harsh Getae. Yet, as you yourself see, I struggle to draw out the verse: but it is made no softer than my fate. When I read it again, I am ashamed to have written, since I see very much worthy to be blotted out, even by me, who made it, as judge. Yet I do not correct it, this labour being greater than to write, and my sick mind endures to suffer nothing hard, Am I, forsooth, to begin to use the file more bitingly, and to call each single word to judgment? Does fortune torment me too little, unless the Lixus into the Hebrus should flow together, and Athos add its leaves to the Alps? The spirit must be spared that has a piteous wound. Oxen draw their scorched necks out from under the yoke. But, I suppose, fruit is at hand, the most just cause of labours, and the field returns the sown crops with much interest? Up to this time no work, though you recall all of it, has profited me— and would that it had not harmed me! You wonder, then, why I write? I wonder too myself, and often I ask with you what I seek from it, Does the crowd truly deny that poets are sane, and am I the greatest proof of this saying, who, so often deceived by a barren field, persist in burying seed in the ruinous soil? No doubt each man is greedy of his own pursuits, and it pleases him to spend his time in his accustomed art, The wounded gladiator forswears the fight, and the same man, forgetful of his old wound, takes up arms, the shipwrecked man says he will have nothing to do with the sea's waves, and pulls his oars in the very water where he just sailed. So I steadfastly keep up an unprofitable pursuit, and return to the goddesses I wish I had not cultivated. What should I do rather? I am not one to spend my time in slothful leisure: idle time is held by me to be death. Nor does it please me to grow soft till daylight with too much wine, nor does the alluring dice hold my unsteady hands, When I have given to sleep the hours the body demands, how, waking, shall I lay out the long stretches of time? Or shall I, forgetful of my country's custom, learn to bend Sarmatian bows, and be drawn on by the art of the place? This pursuit too my strength forbids me to take up, and my mind is stronger than my slender body, When you have well inquired what I do, nothing is more useful than these arts, which have no usefulness at all. From them I gain forgetfulness of my own misfortune; it is enough if my soil returns me this harvest. Let glory spur you on, you who, that your poems may be approved when recited, keep watch over the Pierian choirs, It is enough for me to compose what comes easily, and the cause of too-intent labour is absent, Why should I polish my poems with anxious care? Or am I to fear that the Getan will not approve them? Perhaps I shall do it boldly, but I boast that the Hister has no greater talent than mine. This is enough, if I attain it in the soil where I must live, to be a poet among the inhuman Getae. Why should I strive for fame into a different part of the world? Let the place fortune has given me be my Rome. With this theatre my unhappy Muse is content: so I deserved, so the great gods willed. Nor do I think there is a way from here to there for my little books, to which Boreas comes with failing wing; we are sundered by sky, and the Bear, far from the city of Quirinus, looks close upon the shaggy Getae. Through so much land, so many waters, I can scarcely believe that the token of my study has leapt across. Suppose it is read, and—what is wonderful—suppose it pleases: that affair surely profits the author nothing, What good would it do you to be praised in hot Syene, or where the Indian water tinges Taprobane? Do you wish to go higher? If the constellations of the Pleiades, distant far, should praise you, what would you carry off from it? But I do not reach there with my mediocre writings, and fame, along with its master, has fled from the city. And you, to whom I perished when my fame was buried, now too, I think, are silent about my death.

Verses set in unequal numbers I, Naso, send to my Salanus, the greeting placed before them. That it may be ratified I desire, and that the omen approve it by the event, I pray you may, friend, be able to read it while safe. Your candour, in this age a thing almost dead, demands that I make such vows. For though I was joined to you by but moderate acquaintance, you are said to have grieved at my exile, and when you read the poems sent from the Euxine Pontus, your favour, such as they were, helped them; and you wished Caesar's anger toward me to be soon undone, which, if he knew, he himself would allow to be wished, You gave such mild vows in keeping with your character, nor are they on that account less welcome to me. And that you may be the more moved by my ills, most learned man, it is likely from the condition of the place, you will hardly find, believe me, in this whole world a soil that enjoys less of the Augustan peace, yet you both read the verses I build amid fierce battles, and approve them, when read, with a favouring mouth, and you applaud my talent, which flows from a poor vein, and from a brook make great rivers, welcome indeed to my mind are these votes, though you would think the wretched can scarcely please even themselves, yet while I try poems on slight subjects, my talent suffices for the slender matter, lately, as the fame of the great triumph reached here, I dared to undertake a work of so great a mass. The weight and the splendour of the theme overwhelmed me in my daring, nor could I bear the burdens of what I had begun. There the goodwill you might praise will be dutiful: the rest lie weakened by the matter, and if that book by chance reaches your ears, let it feel your guardianship, I entrust to it. Since you will do this, even were I not myself to ask, let my gratitude be added as a slight increase, I am not to be praised, but your heart is, whiter than milk and untrodden snow: and you marvel at others, when you are yourself a marvel, nor are your arts and eloquence hidden. The prince of youth, to whom Germany gives a name, Caesar is wont to have as a sharer of his study. You, an old companion, joined to him from his first years, please him, your character matching your talent.
