With you speaking first, his impulse straightway comes: and he has you to draw out his own words by yours. When you have ceased and mortal mouths have grown quiet, and the roofs have held them, with no long delay, there rises the young man worthy of the name of Iulus, like Lucifer risen from the eastern waters. And while he stands silent, his bearing and face are eloquent, and his becoming dress has the promise of a learned voice, soon, when the delay is broken and the heavenly mouth opened, you would swear the gods above are wont to speak in this manner, and you would say 'this is eloquence worthy of a prince, so much nobility is in his speech.' Though you please this man and touch the stars with your head, you think the writings of a fugitive bard worth having, no doubt there is some concord between talents joined, and each keeps the covenants of his own pursuit: the rustic loves the farmer, the soldier him who wages fierce wars, the sailor the steersman of the doubtful ship. You too, devoted one, are held by devotion to the Muses, and you favour, gifted one, my gift. Our work differs, but it issues from the same springs: each of us is a cultivator of a liberal art, the thyrsus is absent from you, the laurel I have tasted, but yet there must be warmth in both: and as your eloquence gives sinews to my numbers, so brightness comes from us into your words. Rightly, then, you think that poems bordering on your pursuit and the sacred bonds of fellow-service must be protected. For which, that the friend by whom you are judged may remain, I pray together for him to the last moments of your life. And may the world's ruler succeed to his own reins: this same thing the people's vows pray for along with me.

You ask whence the letter you read is sent to you? From here, where the Hister is joined with the dark-blue waters, as the region is named, the author too ought to come to mind, Naso the poet, harmed by his own talent. He sends you, from the shaggy Getae, the greeting which, present, he would rather bring, Maximus Cotta. I have read, O youth not unworthy of your father's voice, the eloquent words spoken by you in the full Forum. Which, although they were read by me with hurrying tongue through enough many hours, I complain were too few. But I made them more by reading them often, nor were they ever not more welcome to me than at the first, and since, read so often, they lose nothing of their sweetness, they please by their own powers, not by novelty. Happy those to whom it fell to know these in the very act and to enjoy so eloquent a mouth! For, although the savour is sweet in water brought to one, the waters are more pleasingly drunk from the spring itself. And it pleases more to pluck the fruit from the drawn-down branch than to take it from an engraved dish. But had I not sinned, had not my Muse driven me into flight, your voice would have shown me the work which I read, and, as I was wont, I should perhaps have sat as one judge of the hundred men upon your words, and a greater pleasure would have filled my heart, when I was drawn on by your words and assented to them. But since fate has preferred that I, my country and you left behind, should be among the inhuman Getae, what is allowed, that I may seem to be more with you, send me often, I pray, the pledges of your study to be read, and follow my example, unless you scorn that very thing, which you yourself could more rightly give to me, for I, who have long since perished, Maximus, to you, strive by my talent not to have perished. Repay me in turn, and let my hands receive the not infrequent records of your labour, welcome to be, yet tell me, O youth full of my studies, whether you are reminded of me by these very things. Whether, when you either recite a poem just made to your friends, or, as you often do, require them to recite, I am missed, so that sometimes your mind, forgetting what is absent, surely feels that something of its own is gone, and as you were wont to speak much of me when I was present, is the name of Naso now too on your lips? For myself indeed, may I perish, violated by the Getic bow (and you see how near is the penalty of perjury), unless, absent, I see you at almost every moment. Thanks that the mind is free to go wherever it will. When I have come here unseen by any into the city, I often talk with you, often enjoy you speaking. Then it is hard for me to say how well it is, and how bright that hour is in my judgment. Then, if there is any faith, received into a heavenly seat, I suspect I am with the fortunate gods. Again, when I have returned here, I leave heaven and the gods above, and the Pontic soil is not far from the Styx, whence, if I strive to return, fate forbidding, take from me, Maximus, hope without profit.

Go, light elegies, to the learned ears of the consul, and bear my words to be read by the honoured man. The way is long, nor do you advance on equal feet, and the earth lies hidden, covered with winter snow. When you have crossed icy Thrace and Haemus shrouded in clouds and the waters of the Ionian sea, in less than ten days you will come to the mistress city, though you do not make the journey in haste. Straightway from there let the Pompeian house be sought by you: none is closer to the Augustan forum. If anyone, as in a crowd, asks who you are and whence, carry any names you please to his deceived ear. For though it be safe, as I think it is, to confess, words of fear surely have less of fiction. Nor will you have a chance of seeing the consul, no one forbidding, when you have reached the threshold. Either he will govern his Quirites, declaring the law, when, seated high, he presses the ivory conspicuous with figures: or he will arrange the public revenues at the set spear, and will not let the resources of the great city be lessened. Or, when the fathers have been called into the Julian temple, he will treat of matters worthy of so great a consul. Or he will bring the accustomed greeting to Augustus and his son, and consult about a duty too little known. All the time free from these Caesar Germanicus will take away. After the great gods he honours him. Yet when he has rested from the throng of these affairs, he will hold out his gentle hands to you, and ask perhaps what I, your parent, am doing. I wish you to give him such words as these: 'He still lives, and confesses that he owes you the life which he holds as a gift from the mild Caesar before, you, when he fled, he is wont with mindful mouth to recall to have shown safe ways through the barbarism: that he did not warm a Bistonian sword with his blood, was brought about by the care of your heart: besides, many gifts also for the guarding of his life were added, that he might not lessen his own resources. For which deserts, that gratitude be returned, he swears that he will be your bondsman for all time. For sooner shall the mountains lack their shady tree, and the straits be without sail-flying ships, and rivers return to their springs in a backward course, than the gratitude for your service can pass away.' When you have said this, ask him to keep his gifts, so will the cause of your journey be accomplished.

Did your heart grow sad when you heard—for a far-off land was holding you—of my misfortunes? Though you may dissemble, Graecinus, and fear to confess it, if I know you well, it is clear that it was sad. An unlovable harshness does not fall within those manners of yours, nor does it any less differ from your studies. By the liberal arts, of which you have the greatest care, hearts are softened and harshness flees. Nor does anyone embrace those arts with better faith, as far as duty and the toil of soldiering allow. Certainly I, as soon as I could feel what I was —for in my stupor I had no mind for a long while— felt this too of my fortune, that a friend was absent, who was to be a great protection to me. Then there were absent, along with you, the consolations of a sick mind, and a great part of my spirit and counsel. But now, with what is left, bring me, I pray, this one help from afar, and aid my heart with your address, which, if you believe anything an unlying friend, should be called foolish rather than wicked. It is neither brief nor safe to write what may be the origin of my fault; my wounds dread to be handled. In whatever way they were done to me, cease to ask: do not stir them, if you wish anything to close. Whatever it is, though it is no crime, yet it must be called a fault. Or is every fault against the great gods a crime? There is, then, Graecinus, hope of lightening the penalty, not left wholly absent from my mind. This goddess, when the deities were fleeing the wicked lands, alone remained on the earth, hateful to the gods. She makes the digger, too, live, though bound with the fetter, and think that his legs will be free of the iron, she makes the shipwrecked man, when he sees no land anywhere, toss his arms in the midst of the waters. Often the skilful care of physicians has abandoned someone, and yet hope does not fall for him, though his pulse fails. Those shut in prison are said to hope for safety, and someone hanging on the cross makes vows. This goddess has not allowed how many men, who bind their own necks with a noose, to perish by the death they planned! Me too, attempting to end my grief with the sword, she reproached and, casting her hand on me, held me back, 'What are you doing?' she said. 'There is need of tears, not of blood, often by these the prince's anger is wont to be bent.' Though, therefore, it is owed nothing to my deserts, yet there is great hope in the goodness of the god. Pray, Graecinus, that he may not be hard to me, and add your words too to my vow. And may I lie buried in Tomitan sand, if it is not clear that you vow these things for me. For doves will sooner begin to shun the tower, wild beasts the caves, flocks the grass, the gull the waters, than Graecinus show himself ill to an old friend, not all things are so overturned by my fates.

Naso, sad, greets in verse from the Euxine waters Graecinus, whom present he was wont to greet with his voice. This is the exile's voice: the letter lends me a tongue, and if it were not allowed to write, I should be dumb. You reprove, as you ought, the sins of a foolish comrade, and teach me that I bear ills less than my deserts. You speak truly, but late, the reproaches of my fault: remit the harsh words to a defendant who has confessed. When I could cross Ceraunia with a straight sail, that I might shun the wild rocks, then I should have been warned. Now what does it profit me, the shipwreck once made, to learn by what way my skiff ought to have run? Rather give arms to be grasped by a weary swimmer, and do not be loath to have put your hand beneath his chin. And this you do, and may you do it, I pray. So may your mother and wife, so may your brothers and your whole house be safe, and what you are always wont to pray for in heart and voice, so may you make all your deeds approved by the Caesars. It will be shameful for you to have brought your help in no part to an old friend amid his wretched affairs, shameful to draw back your foot, and not to stand with tenacious step, shameful to have deserted a labouring ship, shameful to follow fortune and yield a friend to it, and, unless he be lucky, to deny that he is yours. Not so did the sons of Strophius and of Agamemnon live, this was not the faith of the son of Aegeus and of Pirithous: whom the former age admired, the next will admire, at whose applause whole theatres resound, you too, having kept a friend through a hard time, are worthy to have your name among such great men, worthy you are, and, since you earn praise by piety, the gratitude for your service will not be deaf. Believe me, if my song is not to be mortal, you will be often on the lips of posterity. Only continue, Graecinus, faithful to the weary, and let that impulse last into long delays, since you grant this, yet I use the oar in a breeze, nor does it hurt to set the spur to a galloping horse.

Naso sends to his comrade (how nearly he set the name!) this brief song from the Euxine waters, but if too incautious a hand had written who you were, perhaps a complaint would have been born of the kindness. Yet why, when others think this safe, do you alone ask that my songs not name you? How great is Caesar's clemency in the midst of his anger, if you know it not, you can be more certain from me. From this punishment which I suffer I could take nothing away, if I were forced to be the judge of my own desert. He does not forbid anyone to remember his comrade, nor does he forbid me to write to you and you to me. Nor would you commit a crime, if you console a friend and with soft words lighten his harsh fate. Why, while you fear safe things, do you make such reverence become invidious toward the Augustan gods? We have seen men struck by the bolts of lightning sometimes live and recover, Jove not forbidding. Nor, because Neptune had wrecked Ulysses's ship, did Leucothea refuse to bring help to the swimmer. Believe me, the heavenly deities spare the wretched, nor always press the wounded, and without end. Nor is any god more moderate than our prince: Justice tempers his strength. Lately Caesar set her in a temple made of marble, having long since set her in the temple of his own mind. Jupiter hurls rash bolts at many who have not deserved by guilt to suffer punishment. The god of the sea overwhelms how many with his savage waves, what small fraction of them was worthy to be sunk? Since the bravest perish in the battle-line, even with Mars himself as judge, his choice will be unjust. But if by chance you wish to inquire into us, there is no one who would deny that he has deserved what he suffers. Add that the dead, whether by water or by Mars or by fire, no day can ever restore again. Caesar has restored many, or lightened them of part of their punishment: and among the many, I pray, may he wish me to be, But you, since we are a people under such a prince, do you believe there is danger in addressing a fugitive? Perhaps you might justly fear these things under Busiris as master, or him who was wont to burn men shut in the brazen bull, cease to defame a mild spirit with empty fear, why do you dread savage rocks in calm waters? For myself, that I wrote to you at first without a name, I scarcely seem able to be excused, but fear, in my stunned state, had taken away the use of reason, all counsel had given way before the strange ills, and, fearing my fortune, not the avenger's, I myself was terrified by the title of my own name. So far admonished, grant a mindful poet leave to set dear names in his pages. It will be shameful for us both, if you, nearest to me by long acquaintance, are read in no part of my book. Yet, lest that fear be able to break your sleep, I shall be no more dutiful than you wish, and I shall hide who you are, except when you yourself permit: no one shall be forced to have my gift. You only, whom you could safely love even openly, if that thing is doubtful, love in secret.

The letter you read comes to you, Brutus, from those places in which you would not wish Naso to be, but what you would not wish, pitiable fate has willed; ah me! that prevails more than your vows. In Scythia a five-year Olympiad has been passed by me: now the time crosses into a second lustre. For tenacious fortune persists, and, insidious, sets its malignant foot against my vows. You were sure to speak for me, glory of the Fabian race, Maximus, to the Augustan deity with suppliant voice. You die before my prayers, and I think, Maximus, that I am the cause of your death (let me not be worth so much). Now I fear to entrust my safety to anyone: the very aid fell with your death. Augustus had begun to forgive my deceived fault. He left both my hope and the earth at once, yet such as I could, Brutus, about the new heavenly one I gave a song, set far from your shores. Would that this piety profit me, and that there be now a limit to my ills and a milder anger of the sacred house, that you too pray the same I can clearly swear, O Brutus known to me by no doubtful mark. For though you have always shown me true love, yet this love grew in the adverse time. And whoever should see your tears and mine alike, would believe that two were going to suffer punishment. Nature bore you mild to the wretched, nor to anyone did it give a gentler nature than to you, Brutus: so that one who knew not what you avail in the forensic war, would scarcely think that defendants could be despatched by your mouth. No doubt it belongs to the same man, though they seem to fight, to be easy to suppliants, fierce to the guilty, when the vengeance of the severe law has been undertaken by you, your words have venom in each one, as if by dipping. May it fall to enemies to feel how violent you are in arms, and to undergo the weapons of your tongue. Which are filed by you with so fine a care, that all deny the talent to be of that body, but if you see anyone harmed by unjust Fortune, no woman is softer than your spirit. This I especially felt, when a great part of my friends disowned their knowledge of me. Forgetful of them, never forgetful of you, who, anxious, lighten my ills, I shall be. And sooner shall this Hister, too near a neighbour to me, turn its course into its head from the Euxine sea, and, as if the times of the Thyestean feast returned, the chariot of the Sun be driven toward the eastern waters, than any of you, who grieved that I was taken away, charge me ungrateful, as not remembering you.

The letter which you read brought you, Messalinus, in place of words a greeting all the way from the savage Getae, does the place point out its author? Or, unless the name is read, does it lie hidden that it is Naso who writes these words? Is there anyone of your people set lying in the world's farthest part, except me, who pray to be yours? May the gods, far from all who revere and love you, wish to have knowledge of this nation. It is enough for us to live amid ice and Scythian arrows, if a kind of death is to be reckoned as life, let the land press us with war, or the sky with cold, the fierce Getan with arms, winter battle with hail. Let the region hold us, fruitful in neither apple nor grape, and no side of which rests from the enemy. For the rest, may the throng of your worshippers be safe, among whom, as one of a people, I was a small part. Wretched me, if you are offended by these words and deny that I was ever in any way yours! And even if that were true, you ought to pardon one who lied: my boast takes nothing away from your glory. Who, known to the Caesars, does not feign himself their friend? Grant pardon to the weary: you were my Caesar. Yet I do not break in where it is not lawful to go, and it is enough if you do not deny that your halls were not open to me. And though you had nothing more to do with me, surely by your one mouth I shall be greeted, though less than before, Nor did your father deny us his friendship, the encourager of my study, its cause and its torch: to whom I gave both tears, the last gift at the funeral, and writings to be sung in the middle of the Forum. Add that there is a brother, joined to you by as great a love as was among the sons of Atreus and of Tyndareus: he did not disdain me as companion or as friend: if, however, you think these things will not harm him. If not, in this part too I shall confess myself a liar: let rather that whole house be closed to me, but it neither must be closed, nor has any power the strength to ensure that a friend commits no fault. And yet, though I would wish that even the fault could be denied, so no one is unaware that crime is far from me. But unless part of the offence were excusable, the punishment to come would have been small banishment. But he himself saw this, who sees through all things, Caesar, that my offences could be called folly: and in so far as I allowed, and the matter permitted, he spared, and used the fire of his thunderbolt with moderation. He took away neither life nor wealth nor the power to return, if his anger be conquered by your prayers, but I fell heavily; for what is wonderful, if anyone struck by Jove has no slight wound? Even Achilles himself would hold back his powers, the Pelian spear, when thrown, gave heavy blows, since, then, my avenger's own judgment supports me, there is no reason why your door should refuse to know me. It was cultivated, I confess, less than it ought to have been; but this too was in my fates, I believe. Yet the other house did not feel my duty thus: there I was always beneath your household god. And such is your piety that, though it should not honour you yourself, a brother's friend has some claim upon you. What of it, that as gratitude must always be returned to the deserving, so it is to have deserved well of your fortune? But if you permit us to advise what you should wish, pray the gods to grant more than you may repay. And this you do, and, as far as it is allowed to remember, you were wont to be a cause of service to many because of the gifts given. In what number you please, Messalinus, place me again, only let me be a part not alien to your house: and that Naso suffers ills, since he seems to have deserved them, if you do not grieve that he bears them, yet grieve that he deserved them.

My letter wishes first that you be greeted, Atticus, sent from the ill-pacified Getae. Next follows the wish to hear how you fare, and whether, whatever you do, you have a care for me. Nor do I doubt that you do, but the very fear of ills often forces me to entertain needless fears, Grant pardon, I pray, and forgive my excessive fear. Even the shipwrecked man shudders at calm waters. The fish, once hurt by the deceiving hook, thinks the curved bronze lurks beneath all food. Often the lamb flees a dog seen far off and thinks it a wolf, and, unknowing, shuns its own protection. Wounded limbs dread even a gentle touch, and an empty shadow strikes fear into the anxious. So I, pierced by Fortune's unjust darts, conceive nothing but sorrow in my breast. Now it is clear to me that the fates, keeping the courses they have begun, will always go by the ways accustomed to them: that the gods watch lest anything befall me kindly, and I scarcely think that Fortune can be cheated of words. She is at pains to ruin me, and she who was wont to be fickle, now harms me, constant and well assured. Believe me, if I am known to you for a truthful mouth (and let me not be thought to make my misfortunes plain), you will sooner number the ears of the Cinyphian crop, and how many thymes flower on high Hybla, and how many birds rest on moving wings in the air, and how many fish swim in the sea, you will be certain, than the sum of my labours be reckoned for you, which I have suffered by land, which I have suffered by water. No nation in the whole world is more savage than the Getae; yet even they groaned at my ills, which, if I should try to write out for you in mindful verse, will be a long page of my fate to come. I do not, then, fear that I should think you to be feared, whose love has given me a thousand pledges, but because every wretch is a timid thing, and because for a long time the door of gladness has been shut to me. Now my grief has come to be a habit, and, as by falling water with frequent stroke the rocks are hollowed, so I am wounded by Fortune's continuous blow, and a new wound scarcely now has room in me. No more is the ploughshare worn thin by constant use, no more is the Appian way rubbed smooth by curved wheels, than my breast is trodden by the old throng of ills, and I have found nothing to bring me help. By the liberal arts glory has been sought by many: unhappy, I have perished by my own gifts. My former life is free of fault and was lived without stain: that brought me, wretched, no help. A grievous fault is often forgiven at the prayers of one's own: all favour was dumb for me. Some are aided in hard times by presence: this exile, absent, a vast storm overwhelmed. Who would not have shuddered even at Caesar's silent anger? Harsh words were added to my punishments. Flight is made lighter by the season. Cast upon the sea, I underwent the threats of Arcturus and the Pleiades, keels are often wont to feel a calm winter: no wave was fiercer to the ship of Ithaca. The upright faith of my companions could have lightened my ills: the treacherous crew was enriched with my spoils. Places make exile gentler: no sadder land than this lies beneath either pole. It is something to be near one's native bounds: the farthest land, the farthest world, holds me. Your laurel, Caesar, grants peace even to exiles: the Pontic land lies beneath a neighbouring foe. It is sweet to spend time in tilling the fields: the barbarian enemy does not suffer the soil to be turned. Body and mind are aided by the mildness of the sky: with perpetual cold the Sarmatian shore is stiff. There is in fresh water a pleasure not to be envied: a marsh mixed with sea-salt is drunk here. All things fail. Yet the mind conquers all: it makes even the body have strength, that you may bear the burden, you must strive with full effort, or, if you let your sinews be bent, you will fall; and hope too, that the prince's anger can grow mild with delay, keeps me from being unwilling to live, and from failing. And you, the few who give me no small comfort, whose faith has been tested through my ills, keep what you have begun, I pray, and do not desert the ship at sea, and save me at once and your own judgment.

Words fail me, asking so often for the same things, and now I am ashamed that my empty prayers lack an end. I think a weariness comes over you from a song so alike, and that you have all learned by heart what I ask. And you know now what my letter carries, although the wax has not been loosened from its bonds. Therefore let the burden of my writing be changed, that I may not so often go against the way the river hurries. Forgive me, friends, that I hoped well of you: there will now be an end for me of sinning so. Nor let me be called a burden to my wife: who indeed toward me is as upright as she is timid, and too little persevering. This too, Naso, you shall bear: for you have borne worse things. Now no burden can be felt by you. The bull, led from the herd, refuses the plough, and the young heifer draws back her neck from the hard yoke: we, whom fate has been wont to use cruelly, are long since no novices in any ills, we have come to the Getic bounds: let us die in them, and let my Fate go to the end by the path it began. It pleases to embrace hope—which, vain, never pleases— and to think those things to come, if you desire any to happen: the next step after this is to despair of safety with good cause, and to know once, with true faith, that one has perished. We see some wounds become greater by being treated, which it had been better not to have touched. He perishes more gently who is sunk by a sudden wave, than he who wearies his arms in the swelling waters. Why did I conceive that I could be without the Scythian bounds and enjoy a more prosperous land? Why did I ever hope anything gentler for myself? Was my fortune known to me thus? Behold, I am tortured more grievously, and the look of these places, sought again, renews my sad exile and makes it fresh. Yet it is more useful that the zeal of my friends should cease, than that the prayers they brought should have availed nothing, a great thing indeed it is that you do not dare, friends: but if anyone sought it, there was one who would wish to give. Provided Caesar's anger does not deny us this, bravely shall we die in the Euxine waters.

Since you have been sent, Vestalis, to the Euxine waters, to render justice in the places set beneath the pole, behold, you see present in what a field I lie, nor will you be a witness that I am wont to complain falsely. There will be added to my voice, through you, not idle, young man sprung from Alpine kings, faith, you yourself surely see the Pontus grow thick with ice, you yourself see the wines standing in rigid frost; you yourself see how the fierce Iazyx, an ox-driver, leads laden wagons through the midst of the Hister's waters, and you see poisons sent beneath the curved iron, and the weapon having two causes of death. And would that this part had only been beheld by you, not also known to you by your own war! The march is toward the first spear-rank through thick perils, the honour which lately fell to you by desert, though this title be full of profits for you, the very valour itself, immense, will be greater than the rank. The Hister does not deny this, whose water your right hand once made crimson with Getic blood. Aegisos does not deny it, which, retaken at your approach, felt that there was no help in the nature of the place. For—it is doubtful whether better defended by site or by hand— the city was on a high ridge, level with the clouds. The fierce foe had intercepted it from the Sithonian king and, victor, held the wrested wealth, until Vitellius, borne down on the river's wave, brought the standards against the Getae, the soldier disembarked. But for you, bravest offspring of high Donnus, came the impulse to go against the hostile men. Without delay, conspicuous far off in gleaming arms, you take care that brave deeds cannot lie hidden, and with mighty stride you go against the iron and the place and the rocks, more than the winter's hail. Nor does the throng of javelins, sent over you, delay you, nor the weapons that drip with viper's blood. The darts cling with painted feathers in your helmet, and almost no part of your shield is free of a wound, nor does your body happily escape all the blows: but the pain is less than the keen love of praise. Such, at Troy, before the Danaan ships, Ajax is said to have withstood the Hectorean torches, when they came nearer and hand was brought to hand, and the matter could be carried on close with the fierce sword, it is hard to say what your Mars did there, and how many you gave to death and whom and in what ways. Victor, you trod down the heaps made by your sword, and many a Getan lay beneath your set foot. The lesser man fights, by the example of the first spear-rank, and the soldier bears many wounds, makes many, but your valour passes all the others by as much as Pegasus will go before swift horses, Aegisos is conquered, and your deeds, Vestalis, are attested for all time by my song.

Receive a greeting sent by Naso, dear to you, great part of my soul, Severus. And do not ask how I fare. If I should follow out everything, you would weep; it is enough if the sum of my ill is known to you. We live, without share of peace, amid constant arms, the quivered Getan stirring up harsh wars. And of so many banished, I alone am a soldier in exile: the rest of the throng lie safe, and I do not begrudge it, and that you may the more think my little books deserving of pardon, you will read these poems made in the battle-line. There stands an old city, near the bank of two-named Hister, hardly to be approached for its walls and the site of the place. Caspian Aegisos, if we believe themselves about it, founded it, and called the work by his own name. This the fierce Getan, the Odrysians slain in an unforeseen onset, took, and raised arms against the king. He, mindful of his great lineage, which he increases by valour, is at once present, girt with countless soldiery. Nor did he withdraw before, by the deserved slaughter of the guilty, he had crushed the bold spirits of the people. But to you, bravest in our age, may it be granted always to hold the honoured sceptre in your hand. And may—what is even better, for what fuller thing could I wish you— warlike Rome approve you, along with great Caesar. But mindful whence I started, I lament, O pleasant comrade, that savage arms are added to my ills, that I lack you all. Thrust down to the Stygian shores, the risen Pleiad makes the fourth autumn. Nor would you believe that Naso seeks the comforts of city life; yet he seeks them all the same. For now I remember you, sweet friends, in my mind, now my daughter comes to me along with my dear wife: and from my home I turn again to the places of the fair city, and my mind surveys all things, using its own eyes. Now the forums, now the temples, now the theatres roofed with marble, now there comes to mind every portico with its levelled ground. Now the grass of the Campus that looks upon the fair gardens, the pools and the canals and the Virgin's water. But, I suppose, since the pleasure of the city is taken from the wretch, let me at least be allowed to enjoy any countryside! My mind does not long for the lost fields, and the country, fair to see, on Paelignian soil, nor the gardens set on the pine-bearing hills, which the Clodian way, joined to the Flaminian, looks upon. The gardens which I tended for I know not whom, to which I myself was wont to add—nor am I ashamed—spring water to the planted things: where there are, if they live, certain trees planted by me too, but the fruit not to be gathered by my hand. In place of these lost things, would that it might fall to me at least here, an exile, to have a clod of earth to till! I myself, were it but allowed, would graze the goats hanging on the cliff, I myself would feed the sheep, leaning on my staff; I myself, that my heart may not dwell on its usual cares, would lead the country-dwelling oxen under the curved yoke, and would learn the words the Getic bullocks know, and would add to them the threats they are used to, I myself, guiding the plough-handle pressed by my hand, would try to scatter seed on the stirred soil. Nor would I hesitate to clear the weeds with long hoes, and to give the garden, now thirsting, the waters it might drink, but whence is this for me, between whom and the enemy a wall and a closed gate make the least of distinctions? But for you at your birth—at which I rejoice with my whole heart— the fatal goddesses spun the strong threads. Now the Campus holds you, now the portico with its dense shade, now the Forum, in which you spend rare hours. Now Umbria recalls you, and as you make for the Alban hills the Appian way leads you on a hot wheel into the fields. Perhaps here you wish that Caesar may suppress his just anger, and that your villa be my lodging. Ah! it is too much that you ask, friend: wish more moderately, and, I pray, draw in the sails of your prayer. I would have a land nearer be granted, and one liable to no war: a good part of my ills will be taken away.

Caesar with Caesar has lately been restored to me, the gods which you, Maximus Cotta, sent to me; and that your gift might have the number it owes, Livia is there joined to her own Caesars. Fortunate silver, more blessed than any gold, which, though it was but rude metal in value, now has a deity. You could not, by giving me riches, have given greater things, sending three of the heavenly ones before my eyes. It is something to look upon the gods and to think them present, and as if to be able to speak with the true deity. As far as concerns you, I have returned, nor does the farthest land hold me, and, as before, safe, I tarry in the heart of the city. I see the faces of the Caesars, as before I used to see them: there was scarcely any hope of this wish for me; and, as I used to salute the heavenly deity, I salute them. For one restored you have, I think, nothing greater to give, What is lacking to my eyes but the Palatine alone? Which place, Caesar taken away, will be worthless. When I gaze on this, I seem to myself to behold Rome; for it bears the likeness of its own homeland. Am I deceived, or are the faces in the image angry with me, and has the grim form something of one who threatens? Spare me, man greater in virtues than the immense world, and check the just reins of your vengeance. Spare me, I pray, indelible glory of our age, whom your care makes lord of the lands. By the name of your homeland, which is dearer to you than yourself, by the gods never deaf to your vows, and by the partner of your bed, who alone has been found your equal, and to whom your majesty is no burden, and by your son, like you in the image of valour, who by his character can be known to be yours, and by your grandsons, worthy of their grandfather or their father, who advance with great stride by your commands, lighten our punishment by the smallest part and lessen it, and grant a place far from the Scythian foe. And may your deity too, if it is right, Caesar nearest after Caesar, not be unfriendly to my prayers. So may fierce Germany, with frightened face, soon be borne, captive, before your triumphant horses: so may your father live to Pylian, your mother to Cumaean years, and may you long be able to be a son. You too, bride matching your mighty husband, receive the prayers of a suppliant with no harsh ear. So may your husband be safe, so may you have grandsons with offspring, and from your good daughters-in-law what daughters-in-law have borne, so may Drusus, whom dread Germany snatched from you, have been the only doomed part of your childbearing. So may your son, the purple avenger of his brother's funeral, press on betimes on snow-white horses. Grant assent, oh, gentlest deities, to my timid vows. Let it profit something to have gods at hand. At Caesar's coming the gladiator leaves the arena safe, and his face has no slight aid. We too rejoice that, as far as is allowed, we see your faces, that one house has been entered by three of the heavenly ones, happy those who behold not images but the persons themselves, and who see the true bodies of the gods face to face, since this an unprofitable fate has begrudged me, I honour the faces and likeness that art has given. So men have come to know the gods, whom the high air hides, and the form of Jove is worshipped in place of Jove, in short, you who are with me and will be without end, take care that your figure not be in a hated place. For my head will sooner depart from my neck, and I will suffer the light to leave my dug-out eyes, than I be without you, O public deities, snatched from me: you will be the harbour and altar of my flight. You I will embrace, if I am hemmed by Getic arms, and I will follow you as my eagles, as my standards, either I deceive myself and am mocked by too much desire, or the hope of a more favourable exile is at hand. For less and less sad is the face in the image, and the lips seemed to assent to my words. May the forebodings of my timid mind become true, I pray, and may the god's anger, just though it is, be less.

The gifts I was seeking, to send you, attesting my mindful care, the Tomitan field could provide. You are worthy of silver, and worthier too of tawny gold, but when you give, those things are wont to please you. Yet these places are precious for no metal: the foe scarcely lets the farmer dig them. Gleaming purple often borders your garments, but it is not dyed in the Sarmatian sea. The flocks bear hard fleeces, and to use the art of Pallas the Tomitan women have not learned, a woman, instead of wool, grinds the gifts of Ceres, and carries heavy water on her head beneath the load. Here the elm is not clothed with vine-clad tendrils, no fruits weigh down the boughs with their own weight. The misshapen fields bear gloomy wormwood, and the land teaches by its fruit how bitter it is. Nothing, then, in the whole region of the left Pontus was there which my diligence could send. Yet I have sent you Scythian weapons enclosed in a quiver: may they, I pray, become bloody with your foe. These are the reeds, these the little books this shore has, this is the Muse, Maximus, that thrives in our regions! Which, although I am ashamed to have sent, because they seem small, yet take these things sent, I pray, in good part.

A letter, late indeed, you cultivated in studies, Suillius, has come here from you, but welcome to me nonetheless, in which you say that, if dutiful gratitude can soften the gods above by asking, you will bring me aid. Though now you give nothing, I am made debtor to a friend's heart, and I call the will to help a service. Only let that impulse of yours last into the long age, and let your piety not be wearied by my ills. The bonds of affinity make some claim for us, which I pray may always remain unshaken. For she who is your wife is almost a daughter to me, and she who calls you son-in-law calls me husband, ah me, if, having read these verses, you draw down your face, and are ashamed to be my kinsman! But you will be able to find nothing here worthy of shame except my fortune, which has been blind to me. Whether you sift my lineage, knights from the first origin we shall be found, through countless ancestors: or if you wish to inquire what my character is, take away the error, the wretch's: they lack a stain. You only, if you hope anything can be done by praying, entreat the gods you worship with suppliant voice. Your gods are the young Caesar, appease your deities, than this altar surely none is better known to you. That altar never lets the prayers of its priest be vain: hence seek help for my affairs. However small the breeze that aids us there, my swamped skiff will rise again from the midst of the waters. Then I shall bring solemn incense to the swift flames, and shall be witness how much the deities avail. Nor shall I build you a temple, Germanicus, of Parian marble: that ruin plucked away my wealth. Temples shall the houses and blessed cities make for you; Naso, by his wealth, will be grateful by song. A small gift, I confess, is rendered for great ones, when for granted safety we give words, but he who gives the greatest that he could is grateful in abundance, and that piety has reached its own end. Nor does the incense which the poor man pours to the gods from a small censer avail less than that given on a great dish, and a lamb as milky as the victim pastured on Faliscan grass stains, when struck, the Tarpeian hearths. Yet for the service done to princely men through song there is nothing more fitting. Songs perform the heraldings of your praises, and take care that the fame of your deeds not be fleeting. By song valour becomes long-lived, and, free of the tomb, has the knowledge of late posterity. Wasting age consumes iron and stone, and no thing has greater strength than time. Writings bear the years, by writings you know Agamemnon, and whoever bore arms against him or with him, who would know Thebes and the seven leaders without song, and whatever was after these, and whatever was before? The gods too, if it is right to say it, are made by songs, and so great a majesty needs the singer's mouth. So we know that Chaos, sorted out from that mass of earlier nature, has its own parts: so the Giants, aiming at the heavenly realms, were given to the Styx by the avenger's cloud-bearing fire. So victor Liber drew praise from the conquered Indians, Alcides from captured Oechalia. And lately, Caesar, songs have hallowed in some part your grandfather, whom valour added to the stars. If anything living, then, Germanicus, still remains in my talent, it will all serve you. You, a bard, cannot scorn a bard's service: in your judgment that thing has a price. But had not so great a name called you to greater things, you would have been the highest glory of the Muses. But to give us material is greater than songs: nor yet can you wholly desert them. Now you wage wars in numbers, now in numbers you restrain words, and what is work for others, this will be play for you. And as Apollo is sluggish neither at the lyre nor at the bow, but each string comes to his sacred hands, so you lack neither the learned man's nor the prince's arts, but the Muse is mingled with Jove in your spirit. And since that wave has not driven us from it which the hollow hoof of the Gorgonean horse made, may it profit, and bring help, to guard the common sacred rites, and to have laid a hand on the same studies: that I may at last escape the shores too much exposed to the skin-clad Coralli, and the savage Getae: and if my homeland is closed to the wretch, that I may be set in some place less distant from the Ausonian city, whence I may be able to celebrate your recent praises and recount your great deeds with the least delay. That this prayer may touch the heavenly deities, dear Suillius, pray almost on behalf of your father-in-law.

Your letter, which came to me about Celsus carried off, was at once made wet with my tears; and—what is unspeakable to say, and I thought could not happen— your letter was read with unwilling eyes. Nor has anything more bitter reached my ears since I have been in the Pontus, and I pray it never may, Before my eyes, as the image of one present, his likeness clings, and love feigns that the dead man lives. Often my mind recalls his jests, free of seriousness, and his serious affairs often done with clear faith. Yet no times come to me more thickly than those which I would wish had been the last of my life, when my house, suddenly fallen in a great ruin, collapsed and fell upon its master's head. He stood by me when a great part forsook me, Maximus, and he was not himself a companion of fortune, I saw him weeping for my death no otherwise than if a brother were to be laid on the fire. He clung to me in embrace and consoled me as I lay, and ever mingled his tears with mine. Oh, how often, a hated guardian of my bitter life, did he hold back my ready hands from my own destruction! Oh, how often he said: 'The anger of the gods is appeasable: live, and do not deny that you can be pardoned!' Yet this saying was most frequent of his: 'Consider how great a help Maximus is bound to be to you. Maximus will exert himself, and, with the piety that is his, will beg that Caesar's anger not be obstinate to the end; and he will employ his brother's strength along with his own, and every aid he will try, that you may grieve the more lightly.' These words lessened the weariness of my evil life. Take care, Maximus, that they have not been in vain. He used to swear to me that he would come here too, if only you gave him the right of the long road. For he honoured your inner shrine with no other rite than that with which you yourself honour the gods, lords of the earth. Believe me, though you have many friends, being worthy of them, he was not, of the many, less than any one of them, if only it is not wealth nor the famous name of ancestors but probity and talent that makes men great. Rightly, then, we pour out tears for Celsus snatched away, which, when I was fleeing, he gave me while alive: rightly we give verses attesting his rare character, that those to come may read your name, Celsus. This is what I can send you from the Getic fields, this alone is what here may be mine. I could not attend your funeral nor anoint your body, and I am divided from your pyre by a whole world, he who could—he whom you, while you lived, held as a god— Maximus performed every office for you. He held for you the obsequies and the funeral of great honour, and poured spices into your cold bosom, and, mourning, dissolved the unguents with tears poured forth, and covered your bones, buried in the neighbouring earth. And since to the dead he renders what is owed to friends, he can count me too among the dead.

Royal offspring, whose origin of nobility reaches in name all the way to Eumolpus, Cotys, if now the talkative rumour has come to your ears, that I lie in a part of the soil bordering on yours, hear, gentlest of young men, the voice of a suppliant, and bring to a fugitive (for you can) what help you can. Fortune handed me over to you—and that is what I do not complain of— in this one thing not unfriendly to me. Receive my shipwreck on no harsh shore, that the wave may not have been safer than your land. A royal thing it is, believe me, to succour the fallen, and it befits a man as great as you yourself are. This becomes that fortune of yours: which, though it be the greatest, can yet scarcely be equal to your spirit. Power is never beheld in a better light than as often as it does not let prayers be in vain, this that splendour of your lineage demands, this is the work of a nobility sprung from the gods. This both Eumolpus, the most famous founder of your line, and, before Eumolpus, Erichthonius urges upon you. This you have in common with a god, that both, when entreated, are wont to bring help to your suppliants. Will there be any reason why we should deem the deities worthy of accustomed honour, if you take from the gods the will to help? If Jupiter offered deaf ears to one who prayed, why should the victim fall, smitten, before Jove's temple? If the sea granted me no peace as I went, why should I bring fruitless incense to Neptune? If she cheated the vain vows of the labouring husbandman, why should pregnant Ceres receive the entrails of a sow? Nor will the goat give its throat as victim to unshorn Bacchus, if no new wine flow beneath the pressing foot. We pray that Caesar may govern the reins of empire, because he so well takes counsel for his own homeland. Usefulness, then, makes both men and gods great, favouring also with their aids. You too, see that you help one who lies within your camp, O Cotys, offspring worthy of your parent. It is a pleasure befitting a man to save a man, and by no art is favour better sought. Who does not curse Antiphates the Laestrygonian? Or who disapproves the ways of bountiful Alcinous? You have no father like the man of Cassandrea or of the Pheraean race, or him who roasted the inventor by his own art: but as fierce in war and not to be conquered in arms, so, peace once made, never a lover of blood, add that to have faithfully learned the liberal arts softens the character and does not let it be wild, nor is any of kings more equipped by them, or has given more time to gentle studies. Your poems attest it, which, if you take away your name, I would deny a Thracian youth composed; and that under this region Orpheus may not be the only bard, the Bistonian land is proud of your talent. And as you have spirit, when the matter so demands, to take up arms and steep your hand in an enemy's slaughter, and as you are skilled to hurl the javelin from a swung arm and to bend the neck of a swift horse, so, when due time has been given to your father's pursuits, and the work has by chance rested in its own numbers, that your leisure may not waste away in idle slumbers, you stretch a full road toward the shining stars. This too brings me some bond with you: each of us is a worshipper of the same sacred rite. As bard to bard I stretch out arms in entreaty, that your land be faithful to my exile. I came not, guilty of murder, to the shores of Pontus, nor were dire poisons mixed by my hand: nor was my seal-stone convicted of having set a lying mark upon a forged tablet. Nor did I do anything which the law forbids me to commit: yet a fault graver than these must be confessed by me. And lest you ask what it is, I wrote a foolish Art; this forbids my hands to be guiltless. Whether I have sinned besides, do not seek to ask, that my fault may lie hidden beneath the Art alone. Whatever it is, it found the avenger's anger moderate, who took from me nothing but my native soil, and since I lack this, let your nearness now grant that I may be able to be safe in a hated place.

That in these little books there is the same theme, Brutus, you report that someone carps at my songs: that I ask nothing but to enjoy a nearer land, and speak of how I am hemmed in by a dense foe. Oh, how out of many faults one is reproved! If my Muse sins in this alone, it is well. I myself see the faults of my own books, though each man approves his own songs more than is just, the author praises his work: so perhaps Agrius once said that Thersites was of fair appearance. Yet this error does not deceive my judgment, nor do I straightway love whatever I have begotten. Why then, if I see myself failing, do I sin, and suffer the fault to be in my writing, you ask? It is not the same thing to feel and to remove diseases; the feeling is in all, the ill is taken away by art, often, wishing to change some word, I have let it stand, and my powers fail my judgment. Often it irks me (for why should I hesitate to confess the truth to you) to correct and to bear the burden of long labour. The labour itself delights the writer and lessens the labour, and the work, growing, glows with its own breast. To correct is a thing as much more arduous as great Homer was greater than Aristarchus, so it harms the mind with the slow cold of cares and holds back the reins of the eager, running horse. And so may the mild gods lessen Caesar's anger toward me, and may my bones be covered in a peaceful soil, as the bitter look of my fortune sometimes hinders me, trying to bend my cares, and I scarcely seem to myself sane, who make songs, and try to correct them among the wild Getae. Yet nothing in my writings is more excusable than that one theme is in almost all of them. Glad, I have mostly sung glad things; sad, I sing sad. Each time is suited to its own work. What should I write of but the fault of the bitter region, and pray that I may die in a more agreeable place? But though I say the same things so often, I am scarcely heard by anyone, and my words, ignored, lack any profit. And yet, though these are the same things, I have not written to the same persons, and my one voice tries through many to gain help. Or, lest the reader find the same thought twice, was one of my friends, Brutus, to be entreated? This was not worth so much: forgive me confessing it, learned man: the fame of my work is cheaper than my safety. In short, the material which each man has drawn for himself, the poet varies much at his own discretion. My Muse is the witness, too true even, of my ills, and has the weight of an uncorrupted witness. Nor was it my purpose and care that a book be made, but that to each his own letter be given. Afterward I joined them, gathered as best I could, without order: do not think, by chance, this work was chosen by me. Grant pardon to my writings, of which glory was not my cause, but usefulness and duty.

From where it is allowed, not from where it pleases, Graecinus, Naso sends you this greeting from the Euxine shoals, and, sent, may the gods grant it meet that Dawn which will first give you the twelve fasces: that, since without me you will touch the Capitol as consul and I shall be no part of your throng, my letter on the appointed day may take a master's part and perform a friend's duty. And if I had been born under better fates and my wheel ran true on its axle, my tongue would have done the office of greeting you, which now my hand performs through writing, and, congratulating, I should give kisses with sweet words, nor would that honour be less mine than yours. On that day, I confess, I should be so proud, that scarcely any house could hold my pride: and while the throng of the sacred senate girds your side, I, a knight, should be bidden to go before the consul's feet; and although I should wish to be always nearest you, I should rejoice not to have had a place at your side, nor should I be querulous, though I were crushed by the crowd: but it would then be sweet to me to be pressed by the people, I should gaze, rejoicing, how great would be the order of the column, and how long a road the dense throng would hold, and that you may the more know how common things touch me, I should watch what purple covered you. The figures too I should know, shaped on the curule chair, and the whole carved work of the Numidian tusk. But when you had been led to the Tarpeian heights, while the sacred victim fell at your bidding, me too, secretly giving thanks to him, the great god who sits in the midst of the temple would have heard; and I should give incense with a mind fuller than the dish, glad four times over at the honour of your office. Here I should be numbered among your present friends, if only kindly fates gave the city's right, and the pleasure which now is grasped by mind alone, would then have to be perceived by the eyes too. It has not so seemed good to the heavenly ones, and perhaps justly; for what would it profit me to be denied for the sake of punishment? Yet I shall use my mind, which alone is not exiled from its place, and I shall behold your bordered robe and your fasces. That mind will see you now rendering justice to the people, and will feign itself to be present, secretly, at your affairs. Now it will believe you setting up the long returns of the lustre at the spear, and letting all out on exact faith: now making eloquent words in the midst of the senate, seeking what the public good asks: now decreeing thanks to the Caesars above, or striking the white necks of fat oxen. And would that, when you have prayed for better things, you may ask that the prince's anger be appeased toward me! Let the dutiful fire rise at this voice from the full altar, and let the bright tip give a good omen to your vow. Meanwhile, in the part where it is allowed, lest I complain of all, here too I shall pass a festive time at your consulship. There is a second cause of gladness, not yielding to the first, your brother will be the successor of so great an honour. For the command ended for you, Graecinus, at the last of December he takes up on the very first day. And, such is the piety in you, you will bear alternate joys, you in your brother's fasces, he in yours. So you will have been twice consul, he twice consul, and in your house a double honour will be beheld. Which, though it be vast, and warlike Rome sees no command higher than the highest consul, yet the dignity of the bearer multiplies this honour, and the office given has the majesty of the giver. May it be allowed, then, for Flaccus and for you to enjoy such judgments of Augustus for all time. Yet what time will be free from the nearer care of affairs, add your vows, I pray, to my vows. And if the breeze gives any sail, loosen the ropes, that my ship may go out from the Stygian waters. Flaccus lately governed these places, Graecinus, and under that leader the fierce bank of the Hister was safe. He held the Mysian nations in faithful peace, he terrified with the sword the Getae who trust their bow, he, by swift valour, retook captured Troesmis, and stained the Danube with fierce blood. Ask the look of the place and the discomforts of the Scythian sky, and ask by how near a foe I am terrified: whether the slender arrows are smeared with serpent's gall, or a human head becomes a dire victim. Whether I lie, or the Pontus, hardened by cold, freezes over, and the ice holds many acres of the strait, when he tells these things, ask what my repute is, and ask in what manner I pass the hard times. Nor am I here in hatred, nor surely do I deserve to be, nor with my fortune has my mind too been changed. That calm of mind which you used to praise, that old modesty persists in my accustomed face, so I am far off, so here, where the barbarous foe, where fierce arms avail more than laws, brings it about that, through so many years now, Graecinus, no woman or man or boy can complain of anything about me. This makes the Tomitans favour and stand by the wretch: this land, since it is so, must be witnessed by me. They, because they see I wish it, prefer that I depart: yet, out of regard for themselves, they wish me to be here. Nor would you believe me: there are decrees by which they praise me and the public wax makes me exempt from burdens, and though glory is not fitting for the wretched, the neighbouring towns give me the same gift. Nor is my piety unknown: the host land sees that the worship of Caesar is in my house. There stand alike the dutiful son and the wife as priestess, deities now no lighter than the god already made. And that no part of the house be lacking, both grandsons stand, this nearest his grandmother's side, that his father's. To these I give, as often with incense, words of prayer, as often as the day rises from the eastern world. The whole Pontic land, though you ask it, will say I do not feign this, the witness of my duty. The Pontic land knows that I celebrate, with such games as we can, the birthday of the god. Nor is such piety less known to the guests, if the long Propontis has sent any to these waters, he too, under whom the left Pontus had been a province, your brother, will perhaps have heard these things. My fortune is unequal to my spirit, and gladly, poor, I cull slight resources with such a gift. Nor do I give these things to your eyes, removed far from the city. But content with silent piety we are. And yet these things will touch Caesar's ears at some time. Nothing that is done in all the world is hidden from him. You at least know these things, taken up among the gods, and see, Caesar, as the earth is set beneath your eyes. You hear, seated amid the vaulted stars, the prayers which we give with anxious mouth. Perhaps too those songs reach there, which I sent about you, made a new heavenly one. I augur, then, that your deities are bent by these, nor do you without desert have the mild name of Parent.

Naso the exile sends to you, Flaccus, his greeting, if anyone can send a thing of which he himself is lacking, For long love, with cares, makes the spoiled body sick; my languor does not let it keep its strength. Nor is there any pain, nor am I burned with panting fevers, and my pulse keeps the path of its accustomed measure. My appetite is dull, and the dishes set out stir loathing, and I complain when the hour of hateful food comes. Whatever the sea, whatever the land, whatever the air rears, set it before me, there will be nothing there for which I shall hunger. Let well-attending Youth give me with her lovely hand nectar and ambrosia, the liquids and feasts of the gods, yet that flavour would not whet my dulled palate, and the weight would stand long in my idle stomach. These things, though they are most true, I would not dare to write to just anyone, lest he call my ills mere daintiness, For such, forsooth, is my state, such the look of my affairs, that there could even be a place for daintiness! I pray those daintinesses fall to that man, whoever he is, who fears that Caesar's anger upon me may be lighter. Sleep too, which is food in a slender body, does not nourish my empty frame with its office. But I lie awake, and my griefs lie awake without end, the material for which the place itself gives me. You could scarcely, then, recognize my face once seen, and would ask where the colour went that was there before, A little juice comes through to my thin limbs, and my members are paler than new wax. I have not contracted these losses by immoderate wine: you know that almost only water is drunk by me, I am not weighed down with feasts: if I were touched by love of them, yet there is no abundance of them in the Getic places, Nor does the ruinous pleasure of Venus take away my strength: she is not wont to come to mournful beds. The water and the place harm me, and a cause stronger than these, the anguish of mind which is always present with me. Unless you, along with your like-minded brother, relieved this equally, my mind would scarcely have borne the burden of sadness. You are the land, not hard, to a broken skiff, and you bring me the help that many deny. Bring it, I pray, always, since I shall always lack it, as long as Caesar's offended deity is upon me. That he may lessen, not end, the anger we have earned, let each of you beseech your gods as suppliants.

Do you recognize, from the image of the pressed wax, that Naso writes these words to you, Macer? And if the seal-ring is not the token of its author, is the letter known to have been made by my hand? Or does the lapse of time take from you the knowledge of these, and do your eyes not recall the old signs? Though you have forgotten both gem and hand alike, let only your care for me not have fallen from you. This you owe either to our companionship of long years, or because my wife is not a stranger to you, or to the studies which you have used more wisely than I, and, as is fitting, were made guilty by no Art. You sing of whatever was left to eternal Homer, that the Trojan wars may not lack a finishing hand. Naso, too little prudent, while he hands down the art of loving, has the sad reward of his teaching, the master. Yet there are sacred rites in common among poets, though each of us follows a different path: of these I suspect you to be mindful, though we are far apart, and to wish to lighten my misfortunes. With you as guide I beheld the magnificent cities of Asia: Trinacria was seen by my eyes with you as guide. We saw the sky grow bright with Aetnaean flame, which the Giant set beneath the mountain vomits from his mouth, and the Hennaean lakes and the pools of stinking Palicus, and where Anapus mingles Cyane with his waters. And not far from here the nymph who, while she fled the Elean stream, runs even now beneath the sea's surface, hidden. Here a great part of the passing year was spent by me. Alas, how unlike to the Getae is that place! And how small a part are these of the things we both saw, when you made the roads pleasant for me! Whether in a painted boat we furrowed the dark-blue waves, or the chariot bore us on a nimble wheel, often the way seemed short to us by turns of talk, and the words, if you should count them, were more than the steps, often the day was shorter than our talk, and the slow hour fell short for talking through the summer days. It is something to have feared together the perils of the sea, and to have brought joint vows to the gods of the deep. And now to have managed affairs together, now again from those of which one need not be ashamed, to be able to recount our jests, when these come to your mind, though I be absent, in all the years I shall be before your eyes, as just now seen. I myself indeed, though I am beneath the world's hinge, which always stands higher than the flowing waters, yet behold you with the only heart with which I can, and often talk with you beneath the icy axis, here you are, and know it not, and present, most thronged, while absent, and at my bidding you come from the heart of the city to the Getae. Repay me in turn, and, since that region is more fortunate, hold me there always in a mindful heart.

This is the sixth summer now drawn out for me, to be passed on the Cimmerian shore among the skin-clad Getae. What flints, what iron, dearest Albinovanus, do you compare to my hardness? The drop hollows the stone, the ring is worn away by use, the curved ploughshare is rubbed by the pressed soil. Devouring time, then, destroys all things but me: even death, conquered by my hardness, holds back. Ulysses is an example of a too-patient spirit, tossed for two lustres on the doubtful sea. Yet he did not endure all the times of an anxious fate, and there were often calm delays, or was it grievous for six years to have cherished fair Calypso and to have lain with a goddess of the sea? The son of Hippotes receives him, who gives winds as a gift, that the useful breeze may curve the driven sails, nor is it a labour to hear well-singing girls: nor was the lotus bitter to him who tasted it. These juices, which make forgetfulness of one's homeland, I would buy with part of my life, if only they were given. Nor would you ever compare the city of the Laestrygonian to the nations whom the Hister skirts with its slanting water. Nor will the Cyclops conquer savage Piacches in fierceness, who is wont to be how small a part of my terror! Than Scylla, who barks from her trunk with wild monsters at her loins, the Heniochan vessels have harmed sailors more, nor can you compare Charybdis to the hostile Achaeans, though three times she drinks down, three times she vomits up the strait, who, although they roam more freely in the region on the right, yet do not let this side be secure, here are leafless fields, here darts dipped in poisons, here winter makes the straits passable even to the footman, so that, where the oar had just made its way with the beaten waves, the dry wayfarer goes, the ship scorned. Those who come from there say you scarcely believe these things, how wretched he is who bears things harsher than belief! Yet believe; nor will we let you not know the causes why a bristling winter hardens the Sarmatian sea. Nearest to us are the stars that give the shape of the Wain and that have the chief cold. Hence rises Boreas, and he is native to this shore and takes his strength from a nearer place. But the South wind, which breathes warm from the opposite pole, is far off and comes rare and more languid. Add that here rivers are mingled in the enclosed Pontus, and the strait loses its strength through the many a stream. Hither flow Lycus, hither Sugaris and Penius and Hypanis and Cales, and Halys, twisted with frequent eddy, and rapacious Parthenius, and Cynapses, rolling rocks, glides on, and Tyras, slower than no river, and you, Thermodon, known to the female squadrons, and Phasis, once sought by Greek men, and Dyrapses, most clear with the Borysthenian stream, and Melanthus, gently performing his soft course, and he who separates two lands, Asia and the sister of Cadmus, and makes his course between the two, and countless others, among whom the greatest of all, the Danube, denies that it yields to you, Nile, the abundance of so many waters adulterates the waves it swells, nor lets the sea keep its own strength. Nay even, like a pool and a sluggish marsh, its dark-blue colour scarcely exists and is diluted. Fresh water floats on the strait, and is lighter than the sea-water, which has its own weight from the mingled salt. If anyone should ask why these things were told to Pedo, or what it profited to speak them in fixed measures, 'I beguiled my cares and cheated the time,' I shall say. This fruit the present hour has brought me. We have been away, while we write this, from our wonted grief, nor did we feel ourselves to be amid the Getae. But you, I do not doubt, when you praise Theseus in song, that you guard the titles of your material, and imitate the man whom you recount; he surely forbids that faith be a companion of tranquil times only. Who, although he is mighty in deeds and is set down by you, a man to be sung with as great a mouth as he deserved, yet there is something imitable in him for us, and in faith anyone can be a Theseus. You have no enemies to be tamed by sword and club, by whom the Isthmus was scarcely passable to anyone: but love must be shown, no toilsome thing to one who is willing. What labour is it not to have violated pure faith? These things to you, who persist unswerving toward a friend, there is no reason to think said with complaining tongue.

This work, Rufus, Naso, founder of an ill-starred Art, sends to you, hurried in a brief space of time, that, although we are removed far by the whole world's width, you may yet be able to know that we remember you. Forgetfulness of my own name will come to me sooner than your piety be driven from my breast: and I shall give back this soul into the empty airs sooner than the gratitude for your service become vain. A great service I call the tears with which you wetted your face when mine were dry with hardened grief: a great service I call the consolations of a mournful mind, when you gave them to me and to yourself alike, my wife indeed is praiseworthy of herself and on her own account, yet she is made better by your counsel. For what Castor was to Hermione, what Hector to Iulus, this I rejoice that you are to my wife. She strives that she may not be unlike you in probity, and proves herself to be of your blood by her life, therefore what she would have done without any goads, she does more fully, having found you too as her prompter, and the horse, keen and ready of itself to run for the honours of the palm, yet, if you urge it on, will go more bravely, add that you fulfil the charges of one absent with faithful care, and grudge to bear no burden. Oh, may the gods repay you thanks, since we ourselves cannot, who will repay if they see dutiful deeds; and may your body too long suffice for that character, Rufus, the greatest glory of the Fundanian soil.

Gallio, it will be a crime scarcely excusable in me, that you have had no name in my song. For you too, I remember, soothed with your tears my wounds made by the heavenly spear. And would that, hurt by the loss of a snatched-away friend, you had felt nothing further to complain of! Not so did it please the gods, who, cruel, did not hold it an impiety to despoil you of a chaste wife. For a letter, messenger of grief, came to me lately, and your losses were read with my tears. But neither, less wise, would I dare to console the prudent, and to report to you the noted words of the learned: and your grief, if not by reason, I have long suspected to be ended already by the very lapse of time. While your letter comes, while mine, running back, passes through so many seas and lands, a year goes by. It is the office of a fixed time to speak consolations, while the grief is in its course and the sick man seeks help. But when a long day has stilled the wounds of the mind, he who stirs them unseasonably renews them. Add that (and would that the omen come true for you) you can now be happy in a new marriage.

That you are not set among my little books, friend, is brought about by the condition of your name. But I would deem no other worthy of this honour before you— if only my song is any honour. The law of the foot and the fortune of your name stand in the way, and there is no road by which you may enter my measures, for I am ashamed so to split your name into twin verses, that the former end with this part and the lesser begin. And I should be ashamed if, where a syllable lingers, I called you more tightly and named you Tuticanus. Nor can you come into verse in Tuticanus's manner, so that from a long the first syllable be made short, or that be lengthened which now goes out too clipped, and the second be long by a stretched-out delay. If I should dare to corrupt your name by these faults, I should be laughed at and rightly denied to have sense. This was my cause for delaying this gift, which my love will repay with interest added, and I shall sing you by whatever mark, send you songs, known to me almost a boy when I was almost a boy, and through the long series of years which we both have, loved by me no less than brother by brother. You were a good encourager, you were leader and companion, when I guided the new reins with a tender hand. Often I corrected my little books under you as censor, often an erasure was made at my prompting for you, when the Pierian goddesses had thoroughly taught you to compose a Phaeacid worthy of Maeonian pages. This tenor, this concord, begun in green youth, has come unshaken to whitening hair. Which unless they move you, I should think your heart to be of hard iron or closed in unconquered adamant, but sooner shall both war and frosts be lacking to this land, the two things which hateful Pontus has for me, and the North be warm and the South be very cold, and my fate be able to be milder, than your heart be hard to a weary comrade. Let this heap be absent, and it is absent, from my ills. You only, by the gods, of whom that one is surest, under whom your honour has constantly grown as prince, bring it about, guarding the fugitive with constant piety, that the hoped-for breeze not desert my craft. You ask what I charge you with? May I perish, unless it is hard to say; if only he who has perished can perish. Nor do I find what I should do, nor what I would or would not, nor is my own advantage well enough known to me. Believe me, prudence first abandons the wretched, and sense and counsel flee along with the substance, do you yourself, I pray, seek in what part I am to be helped by you, and by what ford you may make a way to my prayers.

O you to be named among my undoubted comrades, who, calling you what you are, Carus, truly, hail! Whence you are greeted, this colour can at once be your token and the structure of my song. Not because it is wonderful, but because it is surely not common: for such as it is, it is not hidden to be mine. I myself too, though you tear the title from the page's front, seem able to say what work is yours. Though set among many little books, you will be known, and through the marked signs will be found out. The strength will profit the author, which we know to be worthy of Hercules and equal to him whom you yourself sing. And my Muse too, caught by her own colour, may perhaps be conspicuous by her own faults. A form so bad forbade Thersites to lie hidden, as fair Nireus was to be gazed upon. Nor will it be fitting for you to marvel if the songs are faulty, which I, almost a Getan poet, make. Ah! I am ashamed, and I have written a little book in the Getic tongue, and barbarian words have been set to our measures: and I pleased (congratulate me) and began to have a poet's name among the inhuman Getae. You ask the subject? Praises: I spoke of Caesar. My novelty was aided by the deity of the god. For I taught that the body of father Augustus had been mortal, that his deity had gone to the ethereal homes: that he was equal in valour to his father, who, when asked, took the reins of empire that he had often refused: that you, Livia, were the Vesta of chaste mothers, doubtful whether more worthy of your son or your husband: that there were two young men, firm supports of their parent, who had given sure pledges of their spirit. When I read these writings through, in a tongue not my country's, and the last page came to my fingers, all moved their heads and their full quivers, and there was a long murmur in the Getic mouth. And someone said, 'Since you write these things of Caesar, you ought to be restored by Caesar's command.' He indeed said it: but the sixth winter beneath the snowy pole now sees me, Carus, banished. Songs profit nothing, songs once harmed me, and were the first cause of so wretched a flight, but you, by the common covenants of the sacred study, by the name of friendship not cheap to you (so may Germanicus, the foe captured in Latian chains, bring material to your talents: so may the boys be well, the common vow of the gods, who have been given you, a great praise, to be shaped), as much as you can, lend weight to my safety, which will be none, unless my place be changed.

These things are sent to you, of whom I lately complained in song that you had a name not fit for my numbers, in which, except that so far I am somehow well, you will find nothing besides that pleases me. Even safety itself is hateful, and it is my last vow, of course, to go from these places to any other you please. I have no care, to what land I be sent from this one, because every one will be more pleasing than the one I see. Into the midst of the Syrtes, into the midst of Charybdis send my sails, provided I lack the present soil. The Styx too, if it is anything, will be well exchanged for the Hister, and anything the world has lower than the Styx, the tilled field hates the grass, the swallow the cold, less than Naso the places next to the Mars-worshipping Getae. For such words the Tomitans are angry at me, and a public anger is stirred by my songs. Shall I, then, never cease to be harmed through my songs, and shall I always be punished by my incautious talent? Shall I, then, that I write not, delay to cut off my fingers, and madly still follow the weapons which harmed me?
