Do I turn aside again to the old rocks and those waters in which my wrecked ship struck? But I have done nothing, no fault is mine, Tomitans, whom, though I loathe your places, I love. Let anyone sift the records of my labour: my letter has complained nothing about you, I complain of the cold and the assaults to be feared from every side and that the wall is battered by the foe, I have said most true charges against the places, not the men. You too often blame your own soil. The Muse dared to teach how his own Ascra was forever to be avoided, that of the old farmer: and he who wrote it had been born in that land, yet Ascra did not swell with anger at her bard. Who loved his homeland more than skilful Ulysses? Yet by his evidence the harshness of the place is taught. Not the places, but the manners the Scepsian harassed with bitter writings, the Ausonian, and Rome was made defendant: yet she endured the false reproaches with an even mind, nor did the fierce tongue harm its author. But a bad interpreter stirs the people's anger against me and calls my songs to a new charge. Would that I were as happy as I am candid of heart! No one wounded by my mouth survives even now. Add that, were I now blacker than Illyrian pitch, the faithful throng was not to be bitten by me. My lot mildly received by you, Tomitans, shows that the Greek men are so gentle. My people, the Paelignian, and my native region, Sulmo, could not have been gentler to my ills. The honour which you would scarcely give to anyone unhurt and safe, was given lately to me by you. I alone so far am exempt on your shores, those excepted who have the gifts of the law. My temples are veiled with a sacred crown, which the public favour, against my will, set on them. As welcome, then, as the Delian land of Latona, which alone gave a safe place to her wandering, so dear to me is Tomis, which to me, driven from my fatherland's seat, remains up to this time a faithful host, would that the gods had granted that it could have the hope of calm peace, and were farther from the icy pole.

If anyone anywhere still survives not forgetful of me, and asks what I, the banished Naso, am doing, let him know that I owe my life to the Caesars, my safety to Sextus: after the gods above, this man will be first for me. For though I embrace all the times of my wretched life, no part of mine is free of his deserts, which are as many in number as the seeds reddening beneath the tough rind in the garden of a fertile field, as many as Africa's crops, as the Tmolian land's clusters, as many as Sicyon's berries, as Hybla bears combs of honey, I confess it: you may witness it, mark it, Quirites! There is no need of the law's force, I myself speak, set me among your father's wealth, a small thing: I am part, however tiny, of your fortune. As your Trinacria and the land once ruled by Philip, as the house joined to the Augustan forum, as your Campania, a countryside pleasing to its master's eyes, and what you hold left to you, Sextus, or bought: so, behold, I am yours, by whose sad gift you cannot say you have nothing in the Pontus, and would that you could, and that a friendlier field be given, and you set your property in a better place! Since this is in the gods' power, try to soften by praying the deities you honour with perpetual piety. For it is scarcely possible to distinguish whether you are the greater proof of my error or its remedy. Nor do I pray as one doubting: but often, with the stream favourable, the course of the going water is increased by oars, and I am both ashamed and afraid to pray always the same things, lest a just weariness come over your mind. But what shall I do? Desire is an immoderate thing. Grant pardon to my fault, mild friend. Often, desiring to write something else, I slip to the same! My letter of itself asks for a place. Yet whether my gratitude is to have effect, or whether the hard Fate bids me die beneath the icy pole, always with unforgetting mind I shall recall your gifts, and my land shall hear that I am yours. And whatever land is set beneath any sky shall hear it (if only my Muse pass the fierce Getae), and shall know you the cause and saviour of my safety, and me yours by less than scale and bronze.

Envy, why do you tear the songs of snatched-away Naso? The last day is not wont to harm talents, and fame comes greater after the ashes, and I had a name even then, when I was numbered among the living; when there were Marsus and Rabirius of the great mouth and Iliac Macer and starry Pedo; and Carus, who would have hurt Juno in his Hercules, if that man were not already Juno's son-in-law, and Severus, who gave Latium a royal song, and both Prisci, with subtle Numa, and you, Montanus, who suffice in unequal numbers or in equal, and have a name by twin song, and he who bade Ulysses write back to Penelope as he wandered for two lustres on the savage sea, and Sabinus, who deserted his Troesmis and the unfinished work of the Days by swift death, and Largus, called by the surname of his talent, who led the Phrygian old man into Gallic fields; and Camerinus, who sings of Troy from conquered Hector; and Tuscus, who has a name from his Phyllis; and the bard of the sail-flying sea, of whom you could believe that the dark-blue gods had composed his songs; and he who told of the Libyan battle-lines and the Roman wars; and Marius, deft in writing of every kind; and the Trinacrian author of his Perseid, and the author, Lupus, of the returning son of Tantalus and of Tyndareus's daughter; and he who turned the Maeonian Phaeacid, and you too, Rufus, lyre-player of the Pindaric lyre; and the Muse of Turranius, leaning on tragic buskins; and your Muse, Melissus, with the light comic slipper; when Varius and Graccus gave fierce words to tyrants, Proculus held the soft path of Callimachus, Passer returned, a Tityrus, to the ancient grasses, and Grattius gave fitting arms to the hunter, Fontanus sang the Naiads loved by the Satyrs, Capella shut his words in unequal measures; and when there were others, all of whose names to recount is a long delay, songs which the common crowd holds; and there were young men, whose work, because it is unpublished, I have no right to name (yet you, Cotta, in the throng I would not dare to keep silent, light of the Muses and bulwark of the forum, to whom, Maximus, redoubled nobility gave the Cottae on your mother's side and the Messallae on your father's) if it is right to say it, my Muse was of bright name and was read among such great men. Therefore cease, Envy, to rail at one removed from his homeland, and do not scatter, bloodthirsty one, my ashes. I have lost all: only life is left, to give me the feeling and the material of ill. What does it profit to send the sword into dead limbs? There is no room in me now for a new wound.
